The bulla-spread phenomenon is when gentle pressure on an intact bulla forces the fluid to spread under the skin away from the site of pressure (Asboe-Hansen s sign, also referred to as the indirect Nlkolsky or Nlkolsky II sign).

question: A patient presents with scaly and crusted lesions on the malar region of the face and in other 'seborrhoeic' areas. Direct lmmunofluoresence shows in vivo lgG and C3 deposition on cell surfaces of keratinocytes as well as the basement membrane zone. Serology shows presence of circulating antinuclear antibodies. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pemphigus erythematosus is a localized variant of pemphigus foliaceus. Scaly and crusted lesions of pemphigus foliaceus are seen on the malar region of the face and in seborrhoeic distribution. The term pemphigus erythematosus describes patients with immunologic features of both lupus erythematosus and pemphigus, i.e. in vivo lgG and C3 deposition on cell surfaces of keratinocytes as well as the basement membrane zone, In addition to circulating antinuclear antibodies.

question: Use of antigen specific ELISA allows for diagnosis of pemphigus. Which of the following best describes ELISA for pemphigus?

choices.C: Serum is positive against Dsg1 but negative against Dsg3 in mucosal-dominant type of pemphigus vulgaris
choices.D: Serum Is positive against Dsgl but negative against Dsg3 In pemphigus vulgaris
choices.E: Serum is negative against both Dsg1 and Dsg3 in mucocutaneous type of pemphigus vulgaris

explanation: Patients serum is tested on ELISA plates pre-coated with recombinant Dsgl or Dsg3 protein leading to detection of specific antibodies against Dsgl or Dsg3. In pemphigus foliaceus the serum is positive against Dsgl but negative against Dsg3. In mucosal-dominant type of pemphigus vulgaristhe serum is negative against Dsgl but positive against Dsg3. In mucocutaneous type of pemphigus vulgaris the serum is positive against both Dsgl and Dsg3. ELISA scores demonstrate parallel fluctuations with disease activity and are useful in monitoring disease activity.

question: A 45-year old patient has severe pemphigus vulgaris. Which one of the drugs used to treat pemphigus has sterility as a side effect?
explanation: Cyclophosphamide is given at a dose of 1-3 mg/kg/day (usually 50-200 mg/day) and its major side effects are haemorrhagic cystitis, sterility and leukopenia. 155 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: A 40-year old man has been diagnosed with lgA pemphigus. Which of the following is the drug of choice in this condition?
explanation: Dapsone is the drug of choice in lgA pemphigus, although colchicine can be used in some cases. A clinical response usually occurs within 24-48 hours. Alternatively, sulphapyrldlne or acltretin can be used. Low- to medium-dose prednisone, or photochemotherapy (PUVA) are other alternatives.

question: Which of the following virus is not been known to be associated with lichen planus (LP)?
explanation: In several case-control studies, the prevalence of HCV was higher in patients with LP than in controls. This association seems to be strongest in Japanese and Mediterranean populations. Of the various types of LP, it is the oral form that is most commonly viewed as a manifestation of HCV infection. Transfusion-transmitted virus (TTV) is highly prevalent in patients with liver diseases, including those with chronic HCV infection. Direct role of TTV in causation of lichen planus is lacking. By in situ hybridization and immunohistochemical techniques, HHV-6 was detected in 67-100% of oral LP lesions and it was absent from normal oral tissues. HHV7 DNA has been demonstrated in lesional samples of lichen plan us more often than non lesional LP.

question: One of the following is not useful in differentiating lichen striatus from linear lichen planus (LP)

choices.A: Histology shows lichenoid changes in lichen planus
choices.B: Hypopigmentation is more often a sequlae of lichen striatus
choices.C: Lichen planus often results in hyperpigmentation
choices.D: Pruritus is more commonly a feature of lichen planus
choices.E: Spontaneous resolution occurs within a short period of time in lichen striatus

correct_text: Histology shows lichenoid changes in lichen planus
explanation: Differential diagnoses of lichen striatus Include linear porokeratosis, linear psoriasis, inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal nevus, linear Darrier s disease, linear LP, blaschkitis and linear GVHD. Linear LP and lichen striatus can occasionally be indistinguishable histologically. Hypopigmentation is a frequent sequela of lichen striatus. Hyperpigmentation appears more commonly associated with LP. Lichen striatus is also characterized by minimal, if any, pruritus, unlike lichen planus which can be very pruritic. Spontaneous resolution occurs within a short period of time in lichen striatus. 156 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: Eccrine sweat glands are present in which one of the following sites?
explanation: External auditory canal, lips, clitoris and labia minora do not have eccrine glands. Apart from the above, approximately 1.6 to 4.0 million eccrine sweat glands are distributed over the entire body skin surface.

question: A patient is said to have chronic urticaria if the urticaria symptoms occur for more than 6 weeks. In addition, which of the following criteria should be fulfilled for urticaria to be classified as 'chronic'?

choices.A: Urticaria occurring at least once a week off treatment
choices.B: Urticaria occurring at least twice a week off treatment
choices.C: Urticaria occurring at least twice a week on treatment
choices.D: Urticaria occurring at least three times a week off treatment
choices.E: Urticaria occurring at least three times a week on treatment

correct_text: Urticaria occurring at least twice a week off treatment
explanation: The term chronic urticaria is applied to continuous urticaria occurring at least twice a week off treatment. Urticaria occurring less frequently than this is called episodic (or recurrent). Episodic urticaria is more likely to have an identifiable environmental trigger.

question: Physical urticarias are induced by an exogenous physical stimulus. Which of the following is the most common physical urticaria?
explanation: Immediate dermographism can be either simple or symptomatic. Simple immediate dermographism occurs in about 5% of normal people. It occurs in response to moderate stroking of the skin. Symptomatic dermographism is the most common type of the physical urticarias. It manifests as linear wheals at sites of scratching or friction. Delayed dermographism often occurs after 30 mins of stroking the skin. Delayed pressure urticaria is characterized by the development of deep erythematous swellings at sites of sustained pressure to the skin, 30 minutes to 12 hours later. Cholinergic urticaria presents with multiple transient papular wheals 2-3 mm in diameter which occur within 15 minutes of physical exertion, hot baths, or emotional stress. Exercise-induced anaphylaxis (EIA) and Food- and exercise-induced anaphylaxis (FEIA) are increasingly recognized syndromes. In FEIA, angioedema and/or anaphylaxis occur within minutes of exercise if it follows either prior ingestion of a specific food (e.g. wheat), or sometimes within 4 hours of a heavy meal. EIA is produced by exercise, but unlike cholinergic urticaria, not by an increase in core temperature induced by other means. 157 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: A 36-year old patient develops an expanding rash on her left thigh after a tick bite. If untreated she is has a highest risk of developing
explanation: Erythema chronlcum migrans is seen in 60-90% of patients diagnosed wich Lyme disease. If untreated, approximately 60% of patients will go on to have oligoarticular arthritis (usually the knee). Approximately 10% develop a neurologic manifestation such as facial nerve palsy. Approximately 5% develop a cardiac complication such as varying degrees of atrioventricular block).

question: Of all the pregnancy associated dermatoses, cholestasis of pregnancy is associated with highest incidence of fetal distress. The risk of fetal distress is highest if levels of maternal bile salts are higher than
explanation: Cholestasis of pregnancy is defined by: - Generalized pru;itus, with or without jaundice. - Absence of viral or drug induced hepatitis. - Absence of primary lesions. - Biochemical abnormalities consistent with cholestasis. - Disappearance of signs and symptoms following pregnancy. - Recurrence during subsequent gestation(s) and oestrogen containing oral contraceptives is common. - Levels of maternal bile salts above 40 µmol/1 are correlated with an increased incidence of fetal (but not maternal) complications. - Meconi um staining and premature labor occur in as many as 45% of patients.

question: In which of the following conditions can you see acantholysis in a skin biopsy?
explanation: Grover s disease characteristically shows acantholysis (separation and rounding off of keratinocytes) with or without dyskeratosis (abnormal keratinlsation). Bullous Pemphigoid is a sub-epidermal disorder with eosinophils. Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic blistering condition with a sub-epidermal split and neutrophilic microabscesses. Erythema multiforme and lupus erythematosus show an interface (lichenoid) reaction pattern.

question: Which of the following cysts lacks a granular cell layer?
explanation: A pilar/ trichilemmal cyst lacks a granular cell layer and shows trichilemmal keratinisation. The cyst is filled with homogenous, eosinophilic keratin unlike the laminated keratin found in an epidermoid cyst. 158 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: Microabscesses are seen in which of the following conditions?
explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis shows papillary neutrophilic microabscesses. Psoriasis can show Munro s microabscesses; these are collections of polymorphonuclear inflammatory cell infiltrate in the stratum cornem/ granular cell layer Pautrier s microabscesses are a localised epidermal collections of atypical lymphoid cells as seen in T-cell lymphoma and mycosis fungoides.

question: Which of the following antibodies Is used to highlight pagetoid spread in superficial spreading malignant melanoma?
explanation: CD31 is a vascular marker. CD30 is a marker for lymphomatoid papulosis and anaplastic large cell lymphoma. MNF116 is a broad spectrum cytokeratin. Alpha SMA (Smooth Muscle Actin) is a marker of smooth muscle tumours and myoepithelial tumours.

question: A 50 year old male presents with a papular skin rash. Histological examination reveals granulomatous inflammation in the dermis. Which of the following markers or special stains will help in the diagnosis
explanation: If there is granulmatous inflammation on skin biopsy an infection should be excluded by performing special stains. Mycobacterium tuberculosis can be visualised using the Ziehl-Neelsen stain. PAS-Aldan blue is a pan-mucin combination. Ber-EP4 and Melan-A are immunohistochemical antibodies. Verhoeff-Van Giesen Stain is an elastic stain.

question: Select the marker most useful in differentiating basal cell carcinoma from basaloid squamous cell carcinoma
explanation: Ber-EP4 is positive in basal cell carcinoma and negative in squamous cell carcinoma. Epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) is positive in squamous cell carcinoma and negative in basal cell carcinoma. CEA is a mc!rker of ductal differentiation. S100 protein, HMB-45 and Melan-A are melanocytic markers. 159 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: A 45 year old female presented with an itchy erythematous rash. Histological examination revealed a spongiotic dermatitis with neutrophils in the superficial keratin layer. Which of the following markers or special stains will help in the diagnosis
explanation: If you see neutrophil polymorphs in the stratum corneum always rule out a dermatophyte infection by performing a PASD (Periodic acid-Schiff stain) with diastase. Diastase removes glycogen in keratinocytes making the fungi easier to see. With PASD the c,ell walls of fungi stain magenta. Alternative fungal stain is Grocott s methenamine silver.

question: A 25 year old female presents clinically with a changing mole. Skin biopsy reveals a lympho-histiocytic infiltrate with residual bland melanocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: A halo naevus on biopsy shows a dense lymphocyttc Infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction which often obscures the melanocyttc component. Reed s naevus is a variant of a Spitz s naevus.

question: A 44 year old female presents with papules showing interface change and Civatte bodies on skin biopsy. What is your preferred diagnosis?
explanation: Lichen plan us has a band of chronic inflammatory cells at the dermo-epidermal junction with numerous Civatte bodies.

question: Which of the following statements about psoriasis is false

choices.A: Histologically shows spongiform pustule of Kogoj
choices.D: Shows interface change on skin biopsy
choices.E: Vascular ectasia is seen with margination of neutrophils

correct_text: Shows interface change on skin biopsy
explanation: Interface change/ lichenoid reaction pattern is not seen in psoriasis. A biopsy showing a combined reaction pattern such as interface change with psoriasiform hyperplasia or psoriasiform hyperplasia with spongiosis etc. one should consider a drug reaction.

question: An infant has a focal area of midline alopecia, overlying a blue-tinged compressible nodule, surrounded by long dark coarse hair. Which of the following investigations would you instigate?
explanation: Features described are those of the hair collar sign; a relatively specific marker of meningoceles and other types of cranial dysraphism. CT or MRI imaging is necessary to determine whether an intracranial connection is present. 160 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: A 31-year old amateur rugby player experiences considerable distress during a dental procedure despite receiving multiple local anaesthetic injections. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: There exists an increasingly well-recognised association between Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, specifically of the hypermobility type, and resistance to local anaesthetics. This can necessitate a higher local anaesthetic dose, a greater time between delivering analgesia and starting surgery, or even consideration for general anaesthesia. The underlying mechanism awaits full elucidation.

question: A 7-year old girl is noted to have exaggerated wrinkling of the palms after brief immersion in water. Which of the following Investigations would you instigate?
explanation: Aquagenic wrinkling of the palms is a cutaneous manifestation of cystic fibrosis that may also be seen in carriers of cystic fibrosis gene mutations. It usually presents with translucent papules that coalesce to form oedematous plaques. Time-to-onset is typically a few minutes, but is usually longer in carriers of cystic fibrosis mutations. The exact cause is unclear and most authorities agree that it is related to dysfunction in sweating. Reported treatments include topical aluminium preparations and botulinum toxin injections.

question: A 15-year old boy, whose family have recently moved to the UK, presents with crops of reddish-brown pigmented plaques and papillomatous lesions over his face, trunk and limbs. These first appeared aged 12 and have steadily grown more extensive. A diagnosis of epidermodysplasia verruciformis is suspected. This disorder results from mutation in which gene?
explanation: Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (or Lewandowsky-Lutz dysplasia) is a rare disorder, typically inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion. Mutations in EVER 1 or 2 genes result in defective cell-mediated immunity. Patients are predisposed to HPV infection and squamous cell carcinoma. Numerous HPV serotypes are associated, although not HPV 16. HPV 5, 8, 10, and 47 serotypes have been isolated in over 90% of epidermodysplasia verruciformis-associated squamous cell carcinomas.

question: Bart-Pumphrey syndrome results from mutation in the gene encoding connexin 26. The function of which structures will be affected?
explanation: Bart-Pumphrey syndrome is characterised by the clinical triad of prominent knuckle pads, leuconychia and deafness. Inheritance is autosomal recessive and arises from mutation in the GJB2/connexin 26 gene. Other disorders resulting from mutation in connexin 26 include Palmoplantar Keratoderma with Deafness and Vohwinkel syndrome. 161 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: A 10-year old girl is seen in clinic with multiple lentigines and blue naevi. During examination, you also elicit a cardiac murmur leading you to suspect an underlying diagnosis of LAMB. To what does the 'A' in this acronym refer?
explanation: LAMB (Lentigines, Atrial Myxomas, Mucocutaneous Myxomas, Blue Naevi) is a type of Myxoma syndrome. Other recognised disorders on this disease spectrum are NAME (naevi, atrial myxomas, rnyxoid neurofibroma, and ephelides) and Carney syndrome (atrial, cutaneous and mammary myxomas, lentigines, blue naevi, endocrine disorders and testicular tumours). Myxoma syndrome may be autosomal dominant or sporadic. One implicated gene in familial cases is PRKAR1A, a cell cycle regulator.

question: You have been reviewing an 18-month year old boy with multiple pa pules over his cheeks and forehead. Initially lesions appeared smooth and pink but lately have developed a yellowish appearance. Diagnostic skin biopsy is consistent with juvenile xanthogranuloma. What action might you consider?

choices.A: None of the above - this is a skin-limited disorder

explanation: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a type of non-Langerhan s cell histiocytosis. It is most commonly seen in male children but can occur in both sexes at any age. Its cause is unknown and diagnosis is confirmed by skin biopsy with collections of, often foamy, lipid-full histiocytes seen in the dermis. There is no associated dyslipidaemia. Ophthalmic involvement, however, can be associated with spontaneous hyphema leading to secondary glaucoma and blindness. Those at greatest risk are children younger than 2 years with multiple skin lesions

question: The second member of a family who have recently installed a hot-tub in their back garden presents to your clinic with follicular-based papules and pustules predominantly distributed over the torso, buttocks and legs. What is the most probable causative agent?
explanation: The number of privately owned hut-tubs in the UK is estimated at 100,000 and is rising. In turn, cases of hot-tub folliculitis - a condition caused by the opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeroginosa and thought to arise from inadequate chlorination - are also increasing. Diagnosis Is largely clinical, with a predominantly truncal eruption appearing within a few days of exposure to contaminated water. Typically, the condition is self-limiting and requires no treatment. Extensive disease, especially in immunosuppressed individuals, may necessitate anti-gram negative systemic therapy. 162 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: A haematology colleague asks for your opinion on a 38-year old female, with newly-diagnosed lupus-related leukopaenia, who now presents with pearly umbilicated papules over her breasts and hands. Her otherwise well 11-month old child has crops of similar lesions. What is the causative agent?
explanation: Molluscum contagiosurn is a DNA poxvirus, as is Orf virus Diagnosis of SLE is based on a combination of clinical findings and laboratory evidence. The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) uses a standard diagnostic classification requiring at least 4 out of the following 11 criteria to be met: Malar rash, discoid rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, non-erosive arthritis, pleuritis or pericarditis, renal dysfunction, neurological dysfunction, haematological disorder (such as leukopaenia), immunological disorder and positive antinuclear antibody.

question: A middle-aged business man who travels extensively abroad has a monomorphic follicular eruption over the face and trunk. Diagnostic skin biopsy demonstrates a dense eosinophilic peri-follicular infiltrate. He denies taking any prescription, over-the-counter or herbal remedies. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: Eosinophilic folliculitis is a feature of cell-mediated immunodeficiency, although nc definitive infective aetiology has been identified. With HIV infection it is seen when the CD4 lymphocyte count falls below 300 cells/ mm3 and typically improves with Highly Active Anti-Retroviral Therapy. Papuloerythroderma of Ofuji or Ofuji disease is a variant of eosinophilic folliculitis that is typically found in Japan and is not associated with immunodeficiency.

question: The case of a 23-year old female medical student, who has recently returned from an elective in Bhutan, is discussed at your local dermato-pathology meeting. She presented with scaly plaques over the shoulders and upper arms alongside systemic upset. Diagnostic skin biopsy demonstrated sarcoidal granuloma, with no plasma cell infiltrate. Both serum ACE and chest radiography have proved reassuring. What next-step investigation will likely be suggested?
explanation: Sarcoidal or naked granulomas consist of loose groupings of epitheloid histiocytes, giant cells and lymphocytes. Asteroid bodies may also be seen within the cytoplasm of macrophages. Differential diagnoses include sarcoidosis and Crohn s disease. Once sarcoidosis has been excluded, colonoscopy would be warranted to exclude metastatic cutaneous Crohn s disease. Secondary syphilis can present with sarcoidal granulomas but the absence of plasma cells points away from this diagnosis. Mycobacterium tuberculosis granulomas classically occur with caseous necrosis. 163 Section l: Answers & Comments

question: A 38-year woman is seen in clinic with extensively sun-damaged skin. She points out well-demarcated and entirely asymptomatic areas of fine pap&r-like wrinkling over her trunk and upper arms that she first noted during a recent pregnancy. No evidence of transepithelial elimination of elastic fibres or fibiosis are seen on diagnostic skin biopsy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Mid-dermal elastolysis is a rare, acquired, skin condition. Focal loss of elastic fibres results from increased elastase enzyme activity. Its exact cause is unknown but associations include ultraviolet radiation, pregnancy and the oral contraceptive pill. It most commonly presents with well-demarcated areas of fine wrinkling but can also manifest with perifollicular papules of reticular erythema. Transepithelial elimination of elastic fibres is a histological feature characteristic of e:astosis perforans serpiginosa, a condition associated with both Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and pseudoxanthoma elasticum. Other associations include Down s syndrome, Marian syndrome, osteogenesis imperfecta, scleroderma, and D-penicillamine. Dermal fibrosis is seen in scarring disorders such as acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans {which also demonstrates dermal atrophy) and cutaneous morphea. Acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans is associated with Lyme s disease.

question: Which of the following structures is involved in the Lewis reaction (also known as the hunter's reflex)?
explanation: The Lewis reaction/ hunter s reflex describes the normal pallor of fingers and other extremities in response to cold. The glomus apparatus or body is a dermal structure consisting of an arteriovenous shunt under autonomic nervous system control. Most numerous in the extremities it plays an important role in temperature regulation by shunting blood away from the skin surface when exposed to cold temperature. The eccrine and pilosebaceous units also play a role in temperature regulation but via sweat production and hair contracture, respectively. The Pacinian corpuscle detects vibration and the Melssner s corpuscle detects fine touch.

question: You wish to undertake a research study to assess circadian variation in keratinocyte RNA levels. Which of the following research techniques would be most appropriate?
explanation: A useful aid-memoire is SNoW DRoP, where southern blotting relates to DNA, Northern blotting to RNA and Western blotting to protein. Eastern blotting allows analysis of post-translational protein modifications (PTM). Reverse PCR would be used to amplify RNA. 164 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: A 23-year man presents with severe facial dermatitis. The problem appeared during a recent camping holiday during which time he used safety matches on a daily basis. Type-4 hypersensitivity has likely developed to which of the following agents?
explanation: Phosphorus sesquisulfide is found in match tips and friction strips of safety matchboxes. The other agents listed are formaldehyde releasers.

question: A 44-year old woman with known chronic plaque psoriasis and metabolic syndrome is suspected to have vulva! psoriasis. Which of the following anatomical structures will most likely be involved?
explanation: Genital psoriasis typically presents in the context of more generalised psoriasis but can present in isolation. Diagnostically helpful features include a symmetrical distribution, marked erythema, occasional fissuring and healing without scarring. First-line treatment is with a weak or moderate potency steroid. Bland emollients play an important role in protecting against chemical and mechanical irritation and subsequent koebnerization.

question: You see a 2-month old child with scarring blistering of the skin. Other features include a mitten deformity with proximal fusion or all hand and toes webs and aphonia. Which of the following combinations concerning 1) inheritance 2) protein(s) affected 3) cellular structure affected and 4) level of the blister, for this condition is true?

choices.A: Autosomal recessive, collagen 7 (COL7A1), anchoring fibril, sublaminal densa
choices.B: Autosomal recessive, laminln 332, anchoring filament, lamlna-lucida split
choices.C: Autosomal dominant, collagen 7 (COL7A1), anchoring fibril, sublaminal densa
choices.D: Autosomal dominant, keratin 5 &14, intermediate filament, intra-epithelial split

correct_text: Autosomal recessive, collagen 7 (COL7A1), anchoring fibril, sublaminal densa
explanation: The clinical features described are those of the autosomal recessive, or Hallopeau-Siemans, type of dystrophic epidermolyis bullosa (EB). Other features include enamel defects and dental caries, nail dystrophy and high propensity to squamous cell carcinoma. Answer C relates to the autosomal dominant form of dystrophic EB, which is less severe and improves with age. Answer B relates to junctional EB, classically subdivided into Herlitz and non-Herlitz types. Answer D relates to EB simplex, which in turn can be subdivided into localised (Weber Cockayne), generalised (Dowling Meara) and superficial types.

question: An 8-year old girl is referred to the department of paediatric dermatology with a port-wine stain overlying her right mid-back. She is under the neurology team for a radiculopathy. You suspect a unifying diagnosis of Cobb Syndrome. Which of the following best describes the inheritance pattern of this condition?
explanation: Cobb syndrome (also known as Cutaneous Vertebral Medullary Angiomatosis or Spinal Arteriovenous Metameric Syndrome) is defined by coexistence of vascular malformations in all tissue layers of a segmental dermatome. Venous or arteriovenous malformations over the back are present from birth may be the only clue to an underlying spinal cord AVM. Neurological manifestations typically involve lower limb motor or sensory deficit and/or sphincter deficits. 165 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: You are asked to review a patient who has developed highly itchy tense blisters around her umbilicus. She is 5 da1;s post-partum and presented with a similar problem after delivery of her first child. You review the histology report a skin biopsy taken at the time. Whai: direct IMf pattern do you anticipate?

choices.E: Linear lgG and C3 at DEJ

explanation: Pemphigoid gestationis occurs with an incidence of approximately 1 in 50,000 in those patients with high risk (DR3 or DR4) HLA types. Other risk factors include a personal history of the disease, Caucasian heritage and other autoimmune disease. There is also a recognised association with choriocarcinoma and hydatidiform moles. The target antigen concerns bullous pemphigoid antigen 2 (BP180). N Presentation may rarely be in the first trimester but is more typically in the second or third trimester or post-partum, as here. An important clinical clue is that the itchy lesions commonly start around the umbilicus, before spreading the rest of the torso and other area,; such as the intertriginous areas and extremities. The face, palms and soles are usually spared. Mucosal involvement occurs in fewer than 20% of cases Diagnosis is with skin biopsy. H&E analysis demonstrates an identical pattern to bullous pemphigoid, with split at theDEJ. Direct IMF shows linear C3 in all cases, with additional lgG only seen in approximately 25% of cases. This contrasts to bullous pemphigoid where the typical pattern on direct IMF is linear lgG and C3 deposition

question: What percentage of patients with linear lgA disease have oral mucous membrane invo!'!ement?
explanation: Linear lgA disease is the commonest autoimmune bullous disease in children. It usually arises spontaneously but sometimes a triggering infection can be identified. The classic presentation is with an annular or crown-of-jewels configuration In adults, the most common association is with medication, especially vancomycin. Other associations include inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatological disorders and both haematological and non-haerr.atologica: malignancy. On skin biopsy, the H&E section demonstrates a sub-epidermal split with neutrophilic infiltrate in a linear fashion, and direct IMF demonstrates linear lgA deposition. This contrasts to dermatitis herpetiformis, where granular neutrophlls predominate The treatment of choice, as with many other lgA-associated neutrophlllc disorders, is Dapsone. Second line agents include sulfa pyridine 166 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: Blue-grey ovoid nests and spoke wheeled pigmentation are evident on dermoscopic examination of a lesion. To which of the following do these features most likely relate?
explanation: Other dermoscopic features of pigmented basal cell carcinomas, relating to melanin inclusion, may include: Absence of a true pigment network, blue-grey dots and globules, homogenous pigmented areas, peripheral leaf-like structures and specks of brown and grey pigment.

question: Ophiasis is recognised to be a poor prognostic marker in alopecia areata. What pattern of hair loss doses it describe?
explanation: Other poor prognostic markers in alopecia areata Include: DQ7 or DR3 haplotype, family history, early/childhood onset, associated atopy (especially with fillagrin gene mutation) or autoimmune disease, extensive hair loss, nail disease (especially dystrophy) and chronicity.

question: A 39-year old patient has an extremely itchy glistening orange-red plaque over the glans penis and foreskin. You suspect a diagnosis of plasma cell (or Zoon's) balanitis. What is the most definitive treatment for thi:; condition?
explanation: The cause of plasma cell balanitis/vulvitis is not known but established risk factors include poor hygiene and being uncircumcised Whilst all the listed treatments listed can be used for plasma cell balanitis, only circumcision is reliably curative

question: What is the risk of developing complicating squamous cell carcinoma in patients with vulval lichen sclerosus?
explanation: Lichen sclerosus is associated with an increased risk of vulva I squamous cell carcinoma, necessitating long-term follow up. By contrast, penile disease is extremely unlikely to progress to squamous cell carcinoma with only one case reported in the literature. Extra-genital disease, typically involving asymptomatic white patches with the appearance of cigarette paper, occurs in around 10 % of cases. There is no associated risk of squamous cell carcinoma at these sites. 167 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: Which of the following photosensitive disorders is typically inherited in a non-autosomal recessive pattern?
explanation: Porphyrias with cutaneous involvement are, without exception, photosensitive and can be classified depending on hepatic and/or e..,1hropoietic involvement. Hepatic porphyrias with cutaneous involvement present with less acute skin changes and concern: 1) Porphyria cutanea tarda: Inheritance: Autosomal dominant {20-30%) or acquired. Enzyme defect: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase 2) Hereditary coproporphyria: Inheritance: Autosomal dominant. Enzyme defect: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase Mixed hepatic dnd erythropoietic porphyria with cutaneous involvement also demonstrates less acute skin change and concerns: 1) Variegate Porphyria. Inheritance: Autosomal dominant. Enzyme defect: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase Erythropoietic porphyrias manifests with acute skin change and concern: 1) Erythropoietic protoporphyria: Inheritance: Mostly autosomal dominant (but autosomal recessive cases have been reported) 2) Congenital erythropoietic porphyria: Inheritance: Autosomal recessive. Enzyme defect: Ferrochelatase 3) X-linked sideroblastic anaemia: Inheritance: X-llnked recessive defect in the ALAS2 gene. Enzyme defect: Erythroid ALA-synthase Other autosomal recessive photosensitive disorders to be aware of Include: - Rothmund-Thompson syndrome - Smith-Lemi-Opitz syndrome - Trichothiodystrophy - Xeroderma pigmentosum

question: What is the trans-epidermal cycle time in normal skin?
explanation: Starting in the basal layer it takes 14 days for the maturing keratinocyte to reach to stratum corneum and a further 14 days to reach to the very surface of this layer, allowing it to be shed. The trans-epidermal time is considerably shorter in diseases such as psoriasis and is prolonged in the elderly. 168 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: A 50-year old woman develops a vesicular eruption over her lower lip after starting PUVA for vitiligo. What is the most likely cause?

choices.A: Photosensitivity due to an associated autoimmune connective tissue disorder
choices.B: Fixed drug eruption to ingested psoralen

explanation: Narrow-band UVB can also elicit HSV reactivation Other side effects shared by both treatment modalities include photo-aging and increased risk of skin ca;icer (although the risk with narrow-band UVB is considerably lower).

question: Which of the following medications is contraindicated in patients with known soya allergy?
explanation: Al!ergy to soya is a contraindication to isotretinoin, as some brands of isotretino:n contain soya oil.

question: Which of the following would you not expect to see on dermatoscopic examination of a seborrhoeic keratosis?
explanation: Other dermoscopic features of seborrhoeic keratoses include: Comedo-like openings, homogenous pigmentation and milia-like cysts. Presence of a pigment network is an atypical feature and raises the suspicion of a seborrhoeic keratosis-like (or verrucous) malignant melanoma.

question: How does the novel oral anticoagulant dabigatran work?

choices.A: Inhibition of activated vitamin K synthesis

explanation: Unlike warfarin, novel oral anticoagulants act independently of the vitamin K pathway and, because of shorter half-lives and more predictable pharmacokinetics, do not require routine therapeutic monitoring Answer B is true for the novel oral anticoagulants rivaroxiban and apixaban Answer A is true for warfarin Answer D is true for heparin

question: A 35-year old man with skin phenotype 2 is to start narrow-band UVB for poorly controlled, chronic plaque psoriasis. What is the maximum number of sessions he can have in a lifetime?
explanation: The maximum number of sessions for narrow-band UVB is 300. A 48-hour gap is needed between each session, allowing 3 sessions per week. For PUVA a maximum of 250 sessions are allowed over a lifetime. A 72-hour gap is needed between each session, allowing 2 sessions per week. 169 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: Which of the following absorbable and non-absorbable suture combinatic;,s will minimise the suture reaction and scarring?
explanation: PDS (polyclioxanone) elicits the greatest scar reaction amongst the absorbable sutures listed and Monocryl the least. Ethllon elicits a greater scar reaction than Prolene. The extent of the scar reaction can also be reduced by using a smaller calibre suture and avoiding delayed suture removal.

question: Question 10: A 55-year patient with a history of self-neglect and features of malnutrition is admitted with an infective exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease necessitating systemic steroids. On day 7 of admission he develops haemorrhagic bullae over his buttocks, groins and inner thighs that break dov.,n to leave deep purulent ulcers. Which causative agent would you expect to identify on blood culture?
Which of the following is the cardinal feature of Mlescher-Melkersson-Rosenthal Syndrome?
explanation: Both Miescher-f,Aelkersson-Rosenthal Syndrome and Melkersson-Rosenthal Syndrome are part of the orofacial granulomatosis disease spectrum, which can demonstrate all the listed features Miescher-Melkersson-Rosenthal Syndrome Is characterised by granulomatous change confined to the lips Melkersson-Rosenthal Syndrome is characterised by granulomatous change involving the lips, tongue together with facial nerve paralysis Strictly speaking, orofacial granulomatosis is a diagnosis of exclusion that can only be made once systemic granulomatous disease such as Crohn disease, sarcoidosis, TB, Wegener s granulomatosis and allergic contact dermatitis have been explored and excluded Food allergies have been proposed to play a role and in some cases a benzoate/cinnamon-free diet can lead to improvement 170 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: A 65-year old lady attends your clinic for review of an itchy erythematous plaque over her right upper chest. Examination under dermoscopy reveals a scattered grey granular pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Lichenoid keratosis is a benign lesion that !s thought to develop from such lesions as a regressing solar lentigo or seborrhoeic keratosis. They typically occur as a solitary lesion on the upper trunk and can resemble superficial basal cell c;:ircinoma, Bowen s disease or even malignant melanoma. The presence of a grey granular pattern under dermoscopy is a clue to diagnosis but alone is not enough to exclude more serious differentials. Histological features include acanthosis and a band-like lichenoid lymphocytic infiltrate. Parakeratosis may also be seen, serving as a distinguishing feature from lichen planus.

question: A GP refers a 17-year old veterinary nurse trainee with suspected Catch Scratch Disease. If her suspicion is correct, what is the likelihood that the patient with have lympadenopathy?
explanation: Catch scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae. Localised, tender lymphadenopathy occurs distal to the ite of a bite or scratch 1-3 weeks after inoculation. A discrete papule or vesicle may also be seen at the site of inoculation. Approximately 50% patients experience systemic symptoms such as fever, headache and malaise. In immunocompetent individuals, the infection is self-limiting, with conservative management appropriate. lmmunocompromised patients, however, are at significant risk of developing complications such as bacillary angiomatosis (a vascular lesion that may extend from the skin and soft tissue into underlying to bone) and require treatment with antimicrobials such as azithromycin.

question: A 19-yecr old patient is referred for review of a lesion overlying her posterior shoulder. Her attention was first drawn to this when planning a tattoo of two intertwined serpents at the site. Examination under dermoscopy reveals streaks of pigmentation forming a peripheral starburst pattern. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation: Spitz or Reed naevi are relatively uncommon, mostly appear during childhood or early adult life. They may be pigmented or non-pigmented. The pigmented variety demonstrates a classic starburst pattern. 171 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: Which of the following vascular patterns would you expect on dermoscopic examination of a dear cell acanthoma?

choices.D: Dot vessels lined up in a string of pearls

correct_text: Dot vessels lined up in a string of pearls
explanation: Clear cell acanthoma (or Degos acanthoma) is a b1:i1ign epithelial skin tumour. Typical presentation ;s with a solitary shiny pink nodule, with wafer-like scaling around its edge. Most common sites are the lower legs. Histology demonstrates epidermal accumulation of clear glycogen-containing cells.

question: A patient is carrying a CTLA-4 gene mutation. Which of the following diseases would you wish to exclude?
explanation: The CTLA-4 protein is found on the surface of cytotoxic r cells and functions ·co down-regulate immune responses. Mutations in the gene encoding this protein predispose to autoimmune disease including coeliac disease, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, autoimmune thyroid disease and lupus erythematosus. Similarly, pharmacological inhibition of CTLA-4, with agents such as ipilimumab, can also trigger autoimmune phenomena.

question: You suspect drug-related Churg-Strauss syndrome in a patient you have oeen treating for chronic urticaria. Which class of drug is likely implicated?
explanation: Use of montelukast, a leukotriene receptor inhibitor, is c1ssociated with a higher incidence of Churg-Strauss syndrome. As with non-drug-related cases, p-ANCA levels can be elevated. Calcineurin inhibitors include ciclosporin (which first must form a complex with cyclophilin-A) Calcineurin inhibition prevents migration of the NFAT transcription factor into the T-cet: nucleus and ultimately results in IL-2 signalling inhibition. The Anti-lgE monoclonal antibody omallzumab has recently been granted a licence for use as a second-line agent for treatment refractory chronic spontaneous urticaria

question: Skin prick testing in a 21-year old female nurse confirms the clinical suspicion of latex allergy. Which of the following factors carries the greatest risk of mortality during any future anaphylactic attack7

choices.D: Strength of skin prick response to latex
choices.E: Family history of death during anaphylaxis

explanation: Poorly controlled asthma is cited as the single most important risk facto, for fatal anaphylaxis, especially in children and young adults, and can be an indication for self-injectable adrenaline. The life-saving intervention during anaphylaxis is adrenaline, delivered via the intramuscular route. In adults the dose is 500 micrograms (0.5 ml of 1:1000 adrenaline). 172 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: You are looking after a patient with cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. At what stage of their disease would you consider introducing Bexarotene?
explanation: Bexarotene is a retinoid receptor agonist. It is often combined AJith other therapies such as PUVA or extrar.orporeal photopheresis. Side effects include hypothyroidism and dyslipldaemla, requiring regular monitoring of thyroid function and lipids.

question: A 29-year old pregnant woman is seen in clinic with her fourth skin malignancy. There is strong family history of cancer with her father and paternal grandmother having suffered medulloblastoma and ovarian cancer, respectively. She and her partner, who has no personal or family of skin cancer, wish to know the likelihood that their child, which they know to be a daughter, will also be affected by the condition. Which of the following is the correct answer?
explanation: Gorlin s syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Non-basal cell carcinoma skin signs can include epidermal cysts, lipomas and palmoplantar cysts. Bony manifestations include bifid ribs, frontal bossing and ontontogenic jaw cysts. Other associated malignancies include medulloblastoma and ovarian cancer.

question: Which of the following statements regarding Vismodegib is true?

choices.A: It inhibits the hedgehog receptor and Its most common side effect is muscle cramps
choices.B: It inhibits the smoothened receptor and its most common side effect is nausea
choices.C: It inhibits the smoothened receptor and its most common side effect is muscle cramps
choices.D: It inhibits the hedgehog receptor and its most common side effect is nausea

correct_text: It inhibits the smoothened receptor and its most common side effect is muscle cramps
explanation: Vismodegib inhibits the smoothened receptor, a key mediator in the Hedgehog signalling pathway. Other commonly-seen side-effects include altered taste sensation anorexia, diarrhoea, fatigue and alopecia.

question: Which HPV serotype is most commonly associated with subungual squamous cell carcinoma?
explanation: Periungual skin is the most common extra-genital site for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Subungal squamous cell carcinoma is commonly a diagnostic challenge, presenting with a variety of nail changes including verruciform hyperkeratosis, dystrophy, longitudinal ridging, onycholysis, erythronychia, subungual haematomas and paronychia. Whilst all subtypes listed are high-risk for subungual squamous cell carcinoma, the most important carcinogenic factor is HPV 16. Longitudinal nail biopsy is the gold standard diagnostic approach as this allows sampling of the nail bed .. matrix and fold. 173 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: What is the second most common site for melanoma in British Caucasian men?
explanation: As reported by the Statistical Information Team at Cancer Research UK, the commonest site for melanoma in men is the trunk (ac.counting for 41% of cases), followed by the head and neck (22%) and arms (19%). For women, the commonest site is the legs (39%), followed by the arms (24%) and trunk (20%).

question: A 14-year old boy with red hair and freckled skin is referred by his GP due to concern regarding a number of atypical moles. On taking a family history you establish that his father, older sister and paternal uncle, all of a similar complexion, had malignant melanoma before the age of 40. Mutation In which gene is most likely to underlie the strong family history of malignant melanoma?
explanation: Hereditary or familial melanoma is currently estimated to account for approximately 10% of all cases of melanoma. It is defined by families in which at least 2 first-degree relatives (or alternatively at least 3 members with any degree of relationship) have had melanoma. Germ-line mutation in the CDKN2A gene, a regulator of cell division, is the most common cause of hereditary melanoma. The lifetime risk for malignant melanoma in someone carrying a CDKN2A gene mutation is nearly 30%. Other heritable mutations that carry an increased risk of malignant melanoma include CDK4, RBl, MDm2TYR, TYRPl, ASIP and MClR genes. The MClR gene encodes the melanocortin-1 receptor. This promotes eumelanin production, thereby controlling the ratio of eumelanin and pheomelanin. Polymorphisms that reduce the ability of the melanocortin-1 receptor result in melanocytes making mostly pheomelanin. These are associated with red hair, fair skin and freckles. Whilst such polymorphisms are associated with increased risk of melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancers, the relative risk is much smaller. Non-inherited or somatic gene mutations that increase the risk of melanoma include those in NRAS, B-RAF and C-KIT. Interestingly, NRAS mutations are more frequent in mucosa! melanomas in the head and neck region, in comparison to B-RAF and C-KIT.

question: A 31-year old woman has BRAF-positive stage 4 malignant melanoma. Which of the following treatments offers her the best prognosis?
explanation: Vemurafenib is a small molecule inhibitor of the 8-RAF enzyme. Delivery is via the oral route. lpilumumab would be first line for BRAF-negative disease. 174 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: A 53-year man has BRAF-negative stage 4 malignant melanoma. Which of the following treatments would afford him the best prognosis?
explanation: lpilimumab is monoclonal antibody that up-regulates immune-surveillance by targeting CTLA-4 (an inhibitory protein on cytotoxic T cells) Delivery is via the intravenous route \/emurafenib would not be indicated for BRAF-negative disease

question: A 31-year old woman is to start lpilimumab for BRAF-negative stage 4 malignant melanoma. What is the most common complicating autoimmune reaction seen with this monoclonal antibody?
explanation: CTLA-4 inhibition can trigger numerous autoi-mmune phenomena The most common of these is autoimmune colitis, manifesting with such symptoms as abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea

question: A patient with stage 4 melanoma presents with her second squamous cell carcinoma since starting a new medication. Which of the following therapies is she most likely to be receiving?
explanation: Dabrafenib and Vemurafenib are 8-RAF enzyme inhibitors. Their most common side effects concern photosensitivity, other skin eruptions and flu-like symptoms. Approximately 25% of patients develop skin cancers, especially squamous cell carcinoma.

question: Which of the following statements regards Naxos syndrome Is most accurate?

choices.A: It is autosomal recessive, involves a defect in the desmoplakin gene, and presents with woolly hair, arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy and striate PPK
choices.B: It is autosomal recessive, involves a defect in the plakoglobin gene, and presents with woolly hair, arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy and diffuse PPK
choices.C: It Is autosomal recessive, Involves a defect In the plakoglobln gene, and presents with woolly hair, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and striate PPK
choices.D: It is autosomal dominant, involves a defect in the plakoglobin gene, and presents with woolly hair, arrhythmogenic left ventricular cardiomyopathy and striate PPK
choices.E: It is autosomal recessive, involves a defect in the plakoglobin gene, and presents with woolly hair, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and diffuse PPK

correct_text: It is autosomal recessive, involves a defect in the plakoglobin gene, and presents with woolly hair, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and diffuse PPK
explanation: Woolly hair may be an inherited as an Isolated condition (usually in an autosomal dominant fashion) or as oart of a syndrome (typically In an autosomal recessive fashion). Answer A is true for Carvajal syndrome.

question: What is the protein target of local anaesthetics?
explanation: Local anaesthetics comprise a lipophilic aromatic region attached to a basic amine side chain. For aminoesters this is via an ester link and for aminoamides this is via amide link. Local anaesthetics block propagation of action potentials of sensory neurons by use-dependent inhibition of voltage-gated Na receptors, binding to a site within the open pore. 175 Section 1: Answers & Comments

question: A 60 year old man, with skin phenotype 3, is referred for urgent review of a solitary plaque on his left shin which he first noticed after a weekend gardening. Dermoscopy shows a central thrombosed lacune. Surrounding this are multiple smaller thrombosed and purple lacunes, over which there is a blue-white veil. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sporadic angiokeratoma typically present as solitary dark red to purple plaques, often with a scaly surface They are composed of dilated capillaries and are often only come to medical attention after trauma leads to bleeding, thrombosis and sudden darkening.

question: Which of the following medications would you wish to avoid in a patient with urticaria! pigmentosa?
explanation: Other medicines that may trigger mast cell degranulation, and thereby worsen mast cell mediated conditions such as urticaria! pigmentosa, include: Amphotericin B, neuromuscular blocking agents such as gallamine, opiates, NSAIDs and aspirin, dextran plasma expander, polymyxin 81 quinine and reserpine. The other medications listed are more classically associated with triggering or worsening psoriasis. 176 Section 2: Paper Section 2: Paper 1

question: Which of the following statements regarding Raynaud's phenomenon is correct?

choices.A: Digital skin colour changes are in the order of red, white, then blue
choices.B: Ergot compounds used in anti-migraine medications improve the condition
choices.C: This is most commonly seen in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus
choices.D: This is most commonly seen in patients with systemic sclerosis
choices.E: This is often associated with interstitial lung disease in the presence of connective tissue disease

correct_text: This is most commonly seen in patients with systemic sclerosis
explanation: Raynaud s phenomenon is most commonly seen in systemic sclerosis, followed by systemic lupus erythematosus and Sjogren s syndrome. The typical digital skin colour changes are white, followed by blue, then red. Ergot compounds, bleomycin, cisplatin and beta blockers tend to worsen this phenomenon. Mechanics hands are seen in dermatomyositis and affect the lateral aspects of the digits. There is a strong association with interstitial lung disease.

question: A 62-year-old man with a background of rheumatoid arthritis presented with red-to-brown plaques and nodules on the dorsal aspect of his hands, which have been present for two months. These are mostly asymptomatic and tend to appear on the metacarpophalangeal joints. Full skin examination showed similar plaques and nodules on both his elbows. There are no associated nail changes. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is incorrect?

choices.A: Histology from these lesions typically shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis
choices.B: Systemic steroids often result in complete resolution of the lesions
choices.C: The condition can be seen in HIV infected patients
choices.D: The condition responds well to treatment with dapsone therapy
choices.E: This condition can be associated with lgA monoclonal gammopathy

correct_text: Systemic steroids often result in complete resolution of the lesions
explanation: The diagnosis here is erythema elevatum diutinum and can be associated with several haematological abnormalities, including lgA monoclonal gammopathy, myelodysplastic syndrome and multiple myeloma. The condition responds generally well to dapsone therapy and poorly to systemic steroids. Histology typically shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with a neutrophilic infiltrate, which may mimic Sweet s syndrome and rheumatoid nodule histologically. In chronic stages, fibrosis and cholesterol deposits are often found.

question: A 41-year-old Caucasian man presented with a three-year history of yellow pa pules coalescing into symmetrical plaques on the axillae, groin and the peri-orbital skin. A biopsy from two separate lesions showed dermal infiltrate with polymorphic cells consisting of foamy histiocytes, which stained negative for CD1a and positive for CD68 and factor XIII. Based on the clinical and histological features, you diagnose xanthomata disseminatum. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is incorrect?

choices.A: Diabetes insipid us can be associated
choices.B: Rectal mucosa I biopsy is often unhelpful
choices.C: The condition responds poorly to topical steroids
choices.D: Lipid profile is often normal in these patients
choices.E: This condition forms part of the Langerhans' cell histiocytosis

correct_text: This condition forms part of the Langerhans' cell histiocytosis
explanation: Xanthomata disseminatum is a non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis and stains negative for both S100 and CD la - markers of Langerhans cells. Foamy histiocytes and the presence of Touton giant cells are often observed. The condition often has normal lipid profile and may be associated with diabetes insipidus due to pituitary involvement. A rectal mucosa I biopsy can be helpful in cases of systemic amyloidosis. Treatment of xanthomata disseminatum is often challenging although agents such as azathioprine, cyclophosphamide and carbon dioxide laser have been used. 209 Section 2: Answers & Comments

question: A 24-year-old man presented with a three month history of asymptomatic generalized maculopapular eruption, on his trunk and extremities. He also had some small, smooth grey patches on his tongue and has been complaining of headaches for four weeks. Further questioning revealed a recent history of unprotected sexual intercourse. Which of the following statements in this condition is correct?

choices.B: Argyll-Robertson pupil is a common finding
choices.C: Histology often shows parakeratosis, lichenoid changes and erythrocyte extravasation in the absence of plasma cells
choices.D: Potential adverse reactions occurring within the first 24 hours of therapy include headache, myalgia and worsening of the eruption
choices.E: Response to Penicillin is generally very poor

correct_text: Potential adverse reactions occurring within the first 24 hours of therapy include headache, myalgia and worsening of the eruption
explanation: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction is an acute febrile reaction that can occur within the first 24 hours of therapy of secondary syphilis. Syphilis responds very well to treatment with penicillin. Dark field microscopy is often of limited value in oral lesions due to the presence of saprophytic spirochetes in the oral cavity. Pupillary constriction with convergence accommodation but no reaction to strong light describes Argyll-Robertson pupils which is a feature of tertiary syphilis. Histologically, secondary syphilis is characterised by a superficial and deep peri- vascular infiltrate containing plasma cells.

question: A 40-year-old woman presented with longstanding translucent yellow, small papules appearing predominantly on her peri-orbital skin. Clinically, you make the diagnosis of syringomas. Which of the following statements is incorrect?

choices.A: Carbon dioxide laser can be used for treating this condition
choices.B: Electron microscopy studies have identified deposits of calcium
choices.C: The eruptive forms can be associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
choices.D: These lesions arise from the intradermal portions of the eccrine sweat ducts
choices.E: These lesions arise from the outer hair root sheath

correct_text: These lesions arise from the outer hair root sheath
explanation: Tricholemmomal cysts arise from the outer hair root sheath. Typically, the histology is of dermal tumours comprising of small ducts of cuboidal cells with moderately eosinophilic cytoplasmic cords set in a fibrous stroma creating a comma-shaped appearance. The eruptive forms of syringomas have also been linked with Marian s and Down s syndromes.

question: Which of the following causes of genital ulceration is not a venereal disease?
explanation: Recurrent genital ulcerations is a minor criterion for the diagnosis of Beh et s disease. Other non-venereal causes of genital ulcerations include trauma, tumours, tuberculosis, aphthosis, vesiculobullous disorders, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and chemical irritants. 210 Section 2: Answers & Comments

question: Which of the following statements regarding pityriasis lichenoides chronica is correct?

choices.A: Histologically, this h2s a similar appearance to pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis Acuta (PLEVA)
choices.B: Phototherapy can be useful in this condition
choices.C: The condition appears predominantly on the face and neck
choices.D: The lesions tend to heal with significant pitted scarring
choices.E: Transformation to cutaneous lymphoma never occurs

correct_text: Phototherapy can be useful in this condition
explanation: Eruotions of pityriasis lichenoides chronica are characterised by erythematous to brown macules or slightly raised papules with fine centrally adherent scale mica scale . Histolog,cally, the appearance is slightly different than PLEVA, which is characterised by a superficial lymphocytic infiltrate, mild parakeratosis and minimal c1:Joptotic keratinocytes. The granular layer is often preserved. Transformation to cutaneous lymphomas has been documented in some cases. This condition tends to affect young adults and is predominantly found on the tn:nk and upper extremities.

question: Borrelia borgderfori has been linked to the pathogenesis of all of the following except
explanation: Rocky mountain spotted fever is caused by Rlckettsla rickettsii and can present with a maculo-papular eruption around the wrists and ankles which may become haemorrhagic and purpuric. Marginal zone B cell lymphoma has been associated with Borrelia in Europe and patients ure often screened for this infection.

question: Which of the following statements regarding eosinophilic cellulitis (Well's syndrome) is correct?

choices.A: Dapsone is the first line treatment
choices.B: Flame figures are pathognomonic of this condition
choices.C: Peripheral eosinophilia is extremely common and is found in almost all cases
choices.D: The condition is often progressive with no spontaneous resolution
choices.E: Vasculitis ls absent on histology and direct immunofluoresence is negative

correct_text: Vasculitis ls absent on histology and direct immunofluoresence is negative
explanation: Systemic corticosteroids are the first line treatment of choice in Well s syndrome. Spontaneous resolution often occurs. Flame figures are found in other eosinophil-mediated dermatoses such as allergic contact dermatitis, bullous pemphigoid and insect bites. Peripheral eosinophilia is found in almost half of the cases. The presence of Peripheral eosinophilia and organ damage should raise the suspicion of hypereosinophilic syndrome. Vasculitis is typically absent histologically with negative direct immunofluorescence. 211 Section 2: Answers & Comments

question: Which of the following statements regarding dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is correct?

choices.A: Chromosomal abnormality, which can be present in this condition, is EWSFLl1
choices.B: Erlotinib can be used in some cases
choices.C: Metastases are extremely common in this condition
choices.D: Positive CD34 with negative Factor Xilla
choices.E: This condition is characterised immunohistochemically by CD34 negative and Factor Xllla positive

correct_text: Positive CD34 with negative Factor Xilla
explanation: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans is a spindle cell tumour with its main differential being dermatofibroma. Dermatofibromas are classically Factor Xllla positive and CD34 negative (the reverse is true for dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans). Chromosomal abnormalities may occur due to translocation of chromosomes 17 and 22, leading to over-expression of platelet-derived growth factor receptor and treatment with imatinib, (particularly if unresectable, recurrent and metastatic), can be used in this condition. Erlotinib is an epidermal growth factor receptor antagonist and can be used in certain cases of solid tumours. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans can metastasise in about 10 - 15% of cases and surgical excision is the first line treatment of choice (Mohs micrographic surgeIy when available).

question: A 57-year-old Caucasian woman presented with a nine month history of a 5 x 5 cm solitary erythematous plaque with overlying telangiectasia on her right shoulder. She did not have any associated pruritus or lymphadenopathy. An incisional biopsy from the plaque showed diffuse dermal subcutaneous lymphocytic infiltrate that spared the epidermis and the cells were positive for CD20, bcl-2 and negative for CD3, CDS, CDlO and bcl-6. The most likely diagnosis here is: aJ Mycosis fungoides.

choices.C: Primary cutaneous B-cell lymphoma of diffuse large cell lymphoma type
choices.D: Primary cutaneous B-cell lymphoma of marginal zone type
choices.E: Primary cutaneous B-cell lymphoma of the follicle centre type

correct_text: Primary cutaneous B-cell lymphoma of marginal zone type
explanation: Cutaneous lymphomas are divided into T and B-cell lymphomas. B-cell lymphomas are sub-divided into diffuse large cell B-lymphoma leg type, marginal B-cell lymphoma and follicle centre. Marginal zone lymphomas are characterised by positivity to bcl-2 and negativity for bcl-6. Follicle centre B-cell iymphomas are characterised by positivity to bcl-6 with negativity to bcl-2. CD20 and CD 79a are both markers of B-cells. B-cell lymphomas, unlike T-cell lymphomas, do not exhibit epiderrnotropism except in rare occasions. Mycosis fungoides is the commonest type of cutaneous T cell lymphoma.

question: A 21-year-old Afro-Caribbean man reported a five year history of persistent painful purulent draining scalp lesions accompanied by p~ogressively worsening alopecia. Physical examination reveals pustules, nodules and fluctuant abscesses, and multiple palpable cervical lymph nodes. Pus was easily drained from some of the abscesses and there were communicating sinuses visible. For this condition, which of the following statements Is incorrect?

choices.A: Anti-fungal treatment is not indicated in this condition
choices.B: Arthralgia may occur in some cases
choices.C: Basal cell carcinoma may complicate long-standing disease
choices.D: Staphylococcus is often the most commonly cultured pathogen from secondarily infected lesions
choices.E: The pathogenesis of this condition relates to primary follicular occlusion disorder

correct_text: Basal cell carcinoma may complicate long-standing disease
explanation: Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp belongs together with hidradenitis suppurativa and acne conglobata to the primary follicular occlusion disorders. Arthralgia can occur in some cases as a systemic manifestation of the disease. Squamous cell carcinoma and not basal cell carcinoma may complicate long- standing disease. Treatment is often disappointing; however there is no role for anti-fungal therapy. 212 Section 2: Answers & Comments

question: A 12-month-old healthy boy was born with a large purplish erythematous raised tumour with central telarigiectasia surrounded by a pale halo on his left upper arm which did not increase in size in the first eight months of his life. At the age of one year, his mother noticed significant flattening of the lesion and fading of the halo. In this condition, which of the following statements is incorrect?

choices.A: Central ulceration is a possible complication In the first few months of life
choices.B: Kasabach-Merritt syndrome occurs In some cases
choices.C: The histology is characterised by small capillary lobules surrounded by dense fibrous tissue with abnormally thin walled blood vessels in the centre
choices.D: This entity is characteristically negative to the immunoreactive glucose transporter-! (GLUT-1)
choices.E: Treatment with oral steroids should be commenced during the first three months of life

correct_text: Treatment with oral steroids should be commenced during the first three months of life
explanation: The diagnosis here is rapidly involuting congenital haemangioma (RICH). Central ulceration, calcification and Kasabach-Merritt syndrome may all occur in this entity. Both RICH and non-involuting congenital haemangioma (NICH) are negative for GLUT- 1; as opposed to infantile haemangiomas that are positive to GLUT-1. Both RICH and NICH are fully developed at birth unlike infantile haemanglomas.

question: Which of the following drugs is most likely to cause drug-induced subacute lupus erythernatosus?
explanation: Thiazide diuretics are the commonest drugs that may cause drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus ,!rythematosus followed by terbinafine, calcium channel blockers and ACE inhibitors. Frusemide is associated with the development of bullous pemphigoid and photosensitivity but not with subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Anti-histone antibodies are positive in around 50% of the cases of drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus as opposed to around 80% in drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus.

question: Sebaceous glands can be found in which cyst walls of the following?

choices.B: Epidermoid cysts & eruptive vellus hair cysts

explanation: Sebaceous cysts are found in steatocystoma multiplex and are absent in the other forms of cysts. Both epidermoid and eruptive vellus hair cysts are composed of epidermal lining. However, in the latter vellus hair can be found in the contents of the cysts. Pilar cysts are composed of the outer hair root sheath lining, which is characterised by absence of t:he granular layer.

question: All of the following drugs can aggravate spontaneous urticaria except
explanation: Several drugs may trigger or aggravate an attack of urticaria which include non- steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, opiates and ACE-inhibitors. Alcohol and stress can have a similar effect. Montelukast is a leukotriene antagonist often used in addition to the anti-histamines in the treatment of urticaria. ACE-inhibitors can also produce isolated angioedema in absence of any wheals due to the inhibition of the breakdown of bradykinin which is different from the urticaria! wheals triggered by ACE-inhibitors through histamine released from mast cells. 213 Section 2: Answers &. Comments

question: Which of the following statements regarding topical retinoids is incorrect?

choices.A: Their use Is associated with increased resistance to the P.acnes bacteria
choices.C: They can exhibit an effect on micro-comedones
choices.E: Stimulation of collagen synthesis may occur

correct_text: Their use Is associated with increased resistance to the P.acnes bacteria
explanation: Topical retinoids are widely used in the treatment of acne due to their effect on comedogenesis, increased collagen synthesis and reduction of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. They can be used in the treatment of melasma due to down-regulation of the tyrosine synthesis which is essential for melanin production. Its use does not lead to increased resistance to the P.acnes to antibiotics. Unlicensed uses of topical retinoids include treating photo damaged skin.

question: A 22-year-old man presented with multiple palpable purpura and petechiae on his buttocks and legs three weeks following a sore throat. He also had symptoms of abdominal pain and ankle swelling. In this condition, which of the following statements is correct?

choices.A: Direct immunofluorescence will show deposition of both lgM and lgG perivascularly
choices.B: Direct immunofluorescence will show lgA deposition peri-vascularly
choices.C: Pulmonary haemorrhage is the commonest co-morbidity in this condition
choices.D: Renal involvement is extremely uncommon and Its presence is often transient
choices.E: The condition is associated with a higher mortality rate in children compared to adults

correct_text: Direct immunofluorescence will show lgA deposition peri-vascularly
explanation: Henoch-Schonlein purpura is an immune-mediated small vessel vasculitis characterised by deposition of lgA complexes In the small blood vessels. It may affect the skin and kidney. The conditon may be recurrent with both skin and renal involvement hence monitoring for up to six months is recommended even in the absence of any positive urinalysis on the initial investigation. The disease in adults has a higher morbidity with the potential for chronic renal involvement compared to children. The commonest organs affected in this condition are the small Joints, kidney, skin and gut wall.

question: Which of the following food allergies are most likely to persist into adulthood when seen in childhood (particularly in the presence of atopic dermatitis)?
explanation: Food allergies are common in children with atopic background which in some children can worsen the eczema or be associated with episodes of urticaria on ingestion of the particular food item. Allergies to peanuts, fish and shell fish are most likely to persist into adulthood. Correct diagnosis of food allergy includes a detailed history compiemented by skin prick testing and RAST testing in selected cases.

question: Which of the following drugs may result in resolution of actinic keratoses?
explanation: Capecitabine is a chemotherapy agent, which is used in the treatment of certain solid tumours. Capecitabine is a pro-drug of 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU), which is well known to be effective in the treatment of actinic keratosis in Its topical form efudlx cream. Hydroxyurea has been reported to induce squamous cell carcinomas in some cases. 214 Section 2: Answers & Comments

question: In which of the following conditions is monoclonal gammopathy usually not found?
explanation: Scleromyxoedema is most likely to be associated with lgG monoclonal gammopathy although other variants may also be possible. Schnitzler s syndrome is most likely to be associated with lgM monoclonal gammopathy. Erythema elevatum diutinum is most likely to be associated with lgA monoclonal gammopathy. Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma can be associated with any sub-type of monoclonal gammopathy. other conditions that may be associated with monoclonal gammopathies include cryogobulinaemia types 1 and 2, Sweet s syndrome and pyoderma gangrenosum.

question: You patch test a 37-year-old woman due to worsening of her eczema despite the use of several topical treatments and found that she has a++ reaction to chlorocresol. Which of the following tieatments can she use safely?
explanation: Chlorocresol is a preservative found in many topical treatments including Eumovate, Betnovate and Fucibet creams. Dermovate cream does contain Chlorocresol but the ointment formula does not and is therefore safe to use in this particular case. Hydrocortisone preparations do not contain Chlorocresol.

question: Which of the following choices is the major criterion for the diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis?

choices.A: Positivity to CD2/CD25 on mast cells
choices.B: Presence of 25% or more mast cells with atypical or spindle-shaped appearance
choices.D: Presence of large mast cell infiltrate in the bone marrow, spleen or liver

correct_text: Presence of large mast cell infiltrate in the bone marrow, spleen or liver
explanation: In order to diagnose systemic mastocytosis one major criterion is required together with the presence of one minor criterion. All the other choices are minor criteria for the diagnosis of mastocytosis. The presence of raised serum tryptase levels in cases of cutaneous mastocytosis may indicate the presence of systemic involvement and may therefore necessitate further investigations. Osteoporosis can occur in cases of systemic mastocytosis. Patients with systemic mastocytosis are at increased risk of developing anaphylaxis and should avoid drugs that can potentially trigger the mast cells. 215 Section 2: Answers & Comments

question: In which of the following drug-induced reactions is facial oedema a common manifestation?

choices.C: Drug reaction with eosinophillia and systemic symptoms

correct_text: Drug reaction with eosinophillia and systemic symptoms
explanation: In acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis small monomorphic pustules may appear on the face however facial oedema often occurs in the setting of drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms. Serum-sickness-like reaction presents with fever, arthralgia and urticaria due to a drug, although unlike serurn-sicirness reaction, vasculitis is not a feature and the complement levels are within normal range. Stevens-Johnson s syndrome atfec.1s the mucosal sites but facial oedema is not a feature of the condition.

question: Which of the following conditions is an example of non-lgE-mediated reactions?
explanation: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a recently recognised condition in which a large number of eosinophils infiltrate the oesophageal mucosa resulting in inflammation. It has been increasingly found in patients with severe atopic disease and presents with dysphagia and reflux disease. Colicky abdominal pain can be mediated through lgE to a food allergen in the absence of skin manifestations. Oral allergy syndrome is a type of lgE-mediated reaction to certain food items, which often cross react with pollen allergy.

question: Which of the following is not a proposed pathogenic mechanism for acne vulgaris?

choices.E: Presence and activity of propionibacterium acne

explanation: The pathogenesis of acne is multifaceted, but four basic steps have been identified: - Follicular epidermal hyperproliferation; - Excessive sebum production; - Inflammation; - The presence and activity of Proµionibacterium acnes.

question: Which of the following chromosomal aberrations Is associated with severe acne?
explanation: The severe form of acne Acne conglobata has been reported to be more common and more severe in X fY chromosomal aberration than in normal subjects. 216 Section 2: Answers & Comments

question: A 54-year old man presents with a squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following is not a risk factor for non-melanoma skin cancers?
explanation: The risk of development of non-melanoma skin cancer depends on genotypic, phenotypic, and environmental factors. The risk is the greatest in residents of high ambient solar irradiance who have markers of ultraviolet (UV) susceptibility, such as light skin, eye, and hair colour, or an inability to tan, and those with benign sun-related skin d;sorders-e.g., actinic keratoses and solar lentigines. The following are risk factors for non melanoma skin cancers: Solar UV radiation, human papillomavirus, iatrogenic immunosuppression, HIV/AIDS and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, PUVA therapy, photosensitising drugs, UVB radiation, ionising radiation, occupational factors, arsenic and tobacco smoking.

question: A 35-year old patier.t with naevoid basal-cell carcinoma svndrome presents with a cluster of basal cell carcinomas on the back. Which of the following treatments is contra-indicated in the treatment of these basal cell carcinomas?
explanation: Patients with naevoid basal-cell carcinoma syndrome have increased sensitivity to radiation and a tendency to develop several basal-cell carcinomas in the irradiated field; radiotherapy is therefore contra-indicated in these patients.

question: A 35-year old man presented with a 6-month history of mouth ulcers and painful blistering eruption on the trunk accompanied by painful warty growths over the groin and axillae. Widespread erythematous and annular plaques with flaccid blisters on trunk and limbs are present along with exophytic plaques on the axillae, groins and peri-anal skin. Extensive erosions are present on the buccal mucosa and papillomatous vegetating lesions on the angles of the mouth. Skin biopsy shows intra-epidermal neutrophilic microabscesses. Direct immunofluorescence shows epidermal intercellular lgG staining and linear and granular C3 at the dermal-epidermal junction. Indirect immunofluoresence on rat bladder epithelium is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pemphigus vegetans (PV) is the rarest variant of pemphigus accounting for 2%- 5.7% of cases. Flaccid bullae or pustules and hypertrophic papillated plaques involve the face, skin folds and oral mucosa. Vegetative and hypertrophic lesions arise from eroded pustules and bullae. The two clinical subclasses of PV; Hallopeau and Neumann type have similar histological and immunofluoresence features.
