It is characterized by crops of painful and tender bright-pink, dermal and subcutaneous nodules arising in clinically normal skin, in association with fever, anorexia, and malaise. Arthralgia and arthritis are commonly seen. Neuritis, adenitis, orchitis/epididymitis or iritis, may rarely be the initial presentation. A neutrophilic leukocytosis is seen. Thalidomide is the treatment of choice. 281 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: Which of the following statements about immunology of bullous pemphigoid is false?

choices.A: Elevated serum lgE levels correlate with the presence of pruritus
choices.B: Peripheral blood eosinophilia correlates with serum lgE levels
choices.C: Peripheral blood eosinophilia is seen In 90% patients
choices.D: Serum lgE is elevated in 50% patients
choices.E: Serum lgE levels correlate with lgG anti-basement membrane zone immunofluorescence titers

correct_text: Peripheral blood eosinophilia correlates with serum lgE levels
explanation: Almost 50% of patients with bullous pemphigoid have elevated total serum lgE. Levels of serum lgE positively correlate with lgG anti-basement membrane zone immunofluorescence titers. Elevated levels of lgE correlate with the presence of pruritus. 90% of patients have peripheral blood eosinophilia. Peripheral blood eosinophilia does not correlate with serum lgE levels.

question: Which of the following is not useful in differentiating epidermolysis bullosa acquisita from porphyria cutanea tarda?

choices.A: Absence of hirsutism in sites affected by epidermolysis bullosa acquisita
choices.B: lgG and complement deposits at the dermo-epidermal junction in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita
choices.C: Immune deposits around the dermal blood vessels in porphyria cutanea tarda
choices.D: Negative urine porphyrin screen in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita
choices.E: Sclerodermoid skin changes and photo distribution of rash in porphyria cutanea tarda

correct_text: lgG and complement deposits at the dermo-epidermal junction in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita
explanation: Epidermolysis bullosa acqulsita may mimic bullous pemphigoid, porphyria cutanea tarda, pseudo-porphyria, bullous lupus erythematosus, cicatritial pemphigoid, linear lgA bullous dermatosis, Brunsting-Perry cicatricial bullous pemphigoid, dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa and rarely other disorders like toxic epidermal necrolysis and dermatitis herpetiformis. Although the presentation of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita may be reminiscent of porphyria cutanea tarda, these patients do not have other hallmarks of porphyria cutanea tarda or pseudo-porphyria, such as hirsutism, a photodistribution of the eruption, or scleroderma-like changes. Urinary porphyrins are within normal limits in epidermolysis bullosa acqulslta. ,u Patients with porphyria cutanea tarda, which may mimic epidermolysis bullosa acquisita clinically, frequently have lgG and complement deposits at the dermo- epidermal junction similar to those of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita patients. Porphyria cutanea tarda skin also demonstrates immune deposits around the dermal blood vessels, which distinguishes it from epidermolysis bullosa acquisita. 282 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: A 23-year old returning traveler presents with a creeping eruption on her foot. All of the following are recognized treatments for this eruption except
explanation: Cut,meous larva migrans infection results in a creeping eruption that occurs when the larvae of dog or cat hookworm (Ankylostoma duodenale and Ankylostoma brazliense) penetrate intact, exposed skin and begin migrating through the epidermis. This gives rise to tingling/prickling at the site of exposure within 30 minutes of penetration of the larvae. Pruritic, erythematous, linear, serpiginious advancing lesions track 3-4 cm from the penetration site. Thiabendazole is the agent of choice in cutaneous larva migrans. Topical application is used for early, localized lesions. The oral route is preferred for widespread eruption. Other effective alternative treatments include oral albendazole, mebendazole, and ivermectin.

question: A 40-year old patient has erosive lichenoid lesions in the oral mucosa. Which of the following is associated with this condition?
explanation: There are reports of association between lichen planus and hepatitis C virus infection, chronic active hepatitis, and primary biliary cirrhosis. Hepatitis should be considered In patients with widespread or unusual presentations of lichen plan us.

question: A 45-year old man has proximal subungual onychomycosis. Which of the following underlying illnesses should be excluded in this patient?
explanation: Proximal subungual onychomycosis is an uncommon variant of dermatophyte infection caused by T. rubrum and is often related to intercurrent disease. Paronychia is not a feature. lmmunosuppressed patients, especially those who are human immunodeficiency vi rus-positive, may present with proximal subungual onychomycosis. Other associations of proximal subungual onychomycosis include peripheral vascular disease and diabetes.

question: Which of the following is the commonest variant of onychomycosis?
explanation: Onychomycosis is classified clinically as distal and lateral subungual onychomycosis (DLSO), superficial white onychomycosis (SWO), proximal subungual onychomycosis (PSO), candidal onychomycosis and total dystrophic onychomycosis. Of these, distal and lateral subungual onychomycosis is the commonest and is most commonly caused by T. rubrum. 283 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: A 70-year old man presents with 20-year history of pigmentation on the lips. Further examination shows linear pigmentation of his fingernails. There is no family history of similar features and his general health has been fine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Laugier- Hunziker syndrome refers to the presence of orolabial pigmented macules and longitudinal melanonychia. It differs from Peutz-Jeghers syndrome in its sporadic occurrence and absence of gastrointestinal involvement.

question: A 50-year old patient is referred with yellow nails. He has a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis. Which of the following statements regarding yellow nail syndrome is incorrect?

choices.A: Can be associated with internal malignancies
choices.B: Can be associated with lichen planus
choices.C: High doses of vitamin E may be helpful
choices.D: Patients report failure of nail growth

correct_text: Can be associated with lichen planus
explanation: Yellow nail syndrome may or may not be associated with a systemic disorder. It is a triad of yellow nails, primary lymphoedema, and pleural effusion. Nail features include thickening, transverse ridging, diminished growth, increased curvature with a hump, and onycholysis. It is occasionally familial. Respiratory tract involvement is seen and features include sinusitis, bronchiectasis, pleural effusions, upper respiratory infections and pneumonia. Other conditions that may be associated with yellow nail syndrome include rheumatoid arthritis and internal malignancies. Patients always claim that their nails have stopped growing. High oral doses of vitamin E may be beneficial. Spontaneous improvement is possible. Topical vitamin E and systemic antifungal medications (itraconazole, fluconazole) do not appear to be effective.

question: Proximal nail splinter haemorrhages are seen in all the following except;
explanation: The following are causes of proximal nail splinter haemorrhages: bacterial endocarditis, trichinosis, anti-phosphollpid syndrome and altitude sickness. 284 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: A 35-year old man presented with a 6-month history of mouth ulcers and painful blistering eruption on the trunk accompanied by painful warty growths over the groin and axillae. Widespread erythematous and annular plaques with flaccid blisters on his trunk and limbs were present along with exophytic plaques on the axillae, groins and peri-anal skin. Extensive erosions were present on the buccal mucosa and papillomatous vegetating lesions on the angles of the mouth. Skin biopsy showed intra-epidermal neutrophilic microabscesses. Direct immunofluorescence and indirect immunofluoresence on rat bladder epithelium were negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Pyodermatitis-pyostomatitis vegetans is a rare disorder characterized by typical mucocutaneous lesions and histopathological changes of pemphigus vulgaris but negative immunofluorescence findings. Clinical and histological differentiation of pyodermatitis-pyostomatitis vegetans from pemphigus vegetans can be impossible. Oral involvement is seen in all cases and cutaneous involvement in around 60% of patients with PD-PSV. The occurrence of pustules on the gingiva is very suggestive of pyostomatitis vegetans. Most patients with PD-PSV have underlying ulcerative colitis (around 50%) or Crohn s disease (around 10%). A prompt response to corticosteroids helps differentiating PD-PSV from PV.

question: Which of the following is not an intra-epidermal blistering process?
explanation: The split in bullous amyloidosis is subepidermal. The blistering in other listed disorders is intra-epidemal. In coma, the blistering may be subepidermal. The thick corneal layers of the palms and soles are responsible for the intact blisters In the epidermis.

question: The blistering process in which of the following disorders Is not subcorneal?
explanation: Toxic epidermal necrolysis results in full thickness epidermal necrosis. Other conditions which result in subcorneal blistering include impetigo, subcorneal pustular dermatosis, infantile acropustulosis, erythema toxicum neonatorum, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosls and miliaria crystalllna.

question: Which of the following is not a recognized side-effect of the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) antagonists?
explanation: The commonest side-effect of EGFRls is the papulo-pustular acneiform eruption; however comedones are typically absent. Pyogenic granulomas and paronychiae are typically late-occurring side-effects (> 3 months). Erythema nodosum can occur following certain drugs with oral contraceptives being the commonest. 285 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: Which of the following conditions is not a true granulomatous disorder?
explanation: Granuloma faciale typically shows a vasculitic histology with no granulomas and the term granuloma here is therefore misleading. A high-index of suspicion may be required to diagnose fish tank granuloma and if suspected, skin biopsy should be sent for mycobacterial cultures which can take several weeks.

question: Which of the following conditions can give a keratoderma-like yellow appearance of the palms?
explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis and pregnancy can give palmar erythema. Limited systemic sclerosis (CREST) gives telangiectasia which can be found on the palms. Hypothyroidism should always be Included in the differentia: of yellow palms particularly when carotinaemia is suspected.

question: The differential diagnosis of "punctate keratoderma" affecting the palms will include all except
explanation: Punctate palmar keratoderma is an autosomal dominant keratoderma characterized by keratotic plugs, often limited to the palmar creases. Cowden s syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition due to PTEN gene defect and can present with palmar keratoses, tricholemmomas, buccal cobblestoning, lipomas, thyroid gland lesions, high-arched palate and adenoid facies. tv Follicular or syringotropic mycosis fungoides can present with palmar involvement but not with punctate keratoses. Although palmar pits are often seen in Darier s disease, this condition can be associated with palmo-plantar keratoses too.

question: A 45-year old lady with type-1 diabetes devek>ps waxy plaques on her shins. You diagnose these as Necrobiosis lipoidica. Which of the following statements regarding necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) is correct?

choices.A: 30% of patients with diabetes will develop NL
choices.B: Less than 1% of diabetes patients will develop NL
choices.C: NL most frequently occurs on the upper trunk

correct_text: Less than 1% of diabetes patients will develop NL
explanation: NL most commonly occurs on the shins and around two-thirds of its sufferers have diabetes. Less than 1% of patients with diabetes develop NL. The condition is difficult to treat and may develop areas of ulcerations. Disease activity appears to be independent from glycaemic control in diabetics. 286 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: You diagnose a patient with pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Which of the following is not a clinical variant/subtype of PG?
explanation: Another variant of PG includes the peri-stomal type which can particularly occur when the underlying inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is active. PG can occur in IBD, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple myeloma and carcinoid tumour (rarely). PG belongs to the group of neutrophilic dermatoses and may respond to corticosteroids, clclosporln and ant1-TNF therapy.

question: A patient presents with nail pigmentation. There is no history of trauma. Which of the following features in a nail would make the diagnosis of acral melanoma more likely than longitudinal melanonychia?
explanation: Digital or acral melanoma can be tricky to diagnose and any suspicious pigmented streak in a nail should be biopsied to exclude this diagnosis. Longitudinal melanonychia is its main differential and often presents with multiple digital involvement, skin type V/VI, narrow bands with c!ear margins, uniform colour, and presence since childhood or puberty. Accompanying nail dystrophy is not a feature in benign melanonychia and should alert the dermatologist to the possible diagnosis of melanoma.

question: Which of the following subtypes of porokeratosis has the highest risk of malignant transformation?
explanation: Porokeratoses are a group of keratinizing disorders characterized histologically by the presence of a cornoid lamella which is a thin column of parakeratotic cells extending through the stratum corneum with absent granular layer and-occasionally- basal layer dyskeratosis. The overall risk of transformation to squamous cell carcinoma is low but is highest with the linear subtype. The commonest variant is disseminated superficial actinic porokeratosis. Giant porokeatosis of Mibelli can also be associated with a higher risk of malignancy transformation. 287 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: A 40-year old man is seen with recurrent oral ulcerations. You suspect Behi;:et's disease. The diagnosis of Beh~et's disease requires the presence of the major criterion and 2 of the minor criteria according to the International Study Group of Beh~et's Disease. Which of the following is the major criterion?

choices.A: A non-follicular (predominantly acral) papulo-pustular acneiform eruption
choices.C: Recurrent genital ulcerations (3 or more) in 12 months
choices.D: Recurrent oral ulcerations (3 or more) per 12 months

correct_text: Recurrent oral ulcerations (3 or more) per 12 months
explanation: Behc;et s disease is a neutrophilic dermatosis with a vasculitis which is more prevalent in the Middle East and Japan. The minor criteria (of which at least 2 are required for the diagnosis) are recurrent genital ulcerations, uveitis or retinal vasculitis, cutaneous involvement (non-follicular papulo-pustular eruption or erythema nodosum) and a positive pathergy test. Joint involvement with arthritis can occur but is not a minor criterion for the diagnosis.

question: A 37-year old man with background of HIV infection presented with a 3-month history of asymptomatic purple-coloured plaques on the lower legs which have failed to respond to topical therapy given by his GP. Biopsy showed a vascular lesion and further immunostaining confirmed the endothelial nature of the lesion. Which of the following is implicated in the pathogenesis of this disease?
explanation: The diagnosis here Is Kaposi s sarcoma which is an angioproliferative tumour arising from endothelial cells. Human Herpes Virus (HHV} 8 is implicated in the pathogenesis. Kaposi s sarcoma has 4 forms: classic, endemic (African}, iatrogenic (secondary to immunosuppressive therapy) and AIDS-related. HHV 8 is also implicated in the pathogenesis of Castleman s disease. HHV 2 is HSV-2 subtype, HHV 4 is Epstein-Barr virus, and HHV 6 is implicated in the pathogenesis of roseola infantum.

question: A 46-year old lady with a chronic eczematous rash on the hands and legs was referred for patch testing by a colleague as she gives a clear history of worsening of her "eczema" following the use of certain products. Patch testing showed a strong reaction to budesonide. Which other steroid preparation should be avoided by the patient?
explanation: Corticosteroids belong to 4 different chemical classes (A, B, C and D) which do not correspond to the potency. Budesonide belongs to group Band therefore all corticosteroids from this group need to be avoided. Group A consists of hydrocortisone acetate and tixocortol pivalate. Group C consists of betamethasone and dexamethasone. Group D1 consists of clobetasol propionate and clobetasone butyrate.

question: A 10-month old baby presented with an 8-month history of a progressively worsening eruption consisting of red-to-light brown patches and plaques on the trunl< and limbs. His mother reported that some of them have blistered, particularly following gentle rubbing. Whilst in clinic you can elicit the Darier's sign on some of the plaques, which of the following should be avoided in this patient?
explanation: The diagnosis is urticaria pigmentosa which is a form of cutaneous mastocytosis. Drugs which can trigger histamine release from mast cells should be avoided and these include NSAIDs, aspirin, opiates, atropine, procaine and polymyxin B. Other forms of cutaneous mastocytosls Include solitary mastocytoma, diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis (rare) and telangiectasia macularis eruptiva perstans. 288 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: Mllia can occur in some genodermatoses and are referred to as "primary milia". Secondary milia can occur in several disorders. In which of the following can milia occur as part of the disease process?
explanation: Milia are benign keratinous cysts. Secondary causes of milia include subepidermal bullous formation (porphyria cutanea tarda, bullous pemphigoid, epidermolysis bullosa acquisita), radiotherapy, thermal burns, acne and allergic contact dermatitis. Porphyria cutanea tarda presents clinically with skin fragility, bullae, erosions, milia and hypertrichosis.

question: A 65-year old woman with end-stage renal failure who attends the haemodlalysis unit developed an indurated tender subctaneous plaque on the Inner aspect of her right thigh. A reticulate pattern of erythema was evident on her thigh. Biopsy from the lesion which Included the subcutaneous fat showed calcification of small vessels with necrosis. In addition to haemodialysis, which other risk factor contributes to the development of this condition?
explanation: Calciphylaxis (also called calcific uraemic arteriopathy ) is a disease with a high mortality rate and occurs in the setting of renal failure, particularly in dialysis- dependent patients. Risk factors include obesity, warfarin use, diabetes mellitus, liver disease, systemic steroid use, raised serum calcium and phosphate product, and raised serum aluminium. Warfarin may alter the balance of calcification promoters and inhibitors and may need to be switched to heparin.

question: A 32-year old man presented with an intensely pruritic follicular eruption on the face r1nd trunk which has not responded to oral flucloxacillln and topical anti-fungal trerapy given to him in the community. A swab frorn 3 follicular pustule showed no growth and a biopsy showed a dense eosinophilic perifollicular infiltrate. The diagnosis of eosinophilic folliculitis was made. Which of the following conditions should he be investigated for?
explanation: HIV infection can have many dermatological manifestations and a diagnosis of eosinophilic folliculitis should be considered in any HIV patient who presents with a pruritic sterile folliculitis in which the biopsy shows an eosinophilic inflammatory cell infiltrate. There are 3 types of eosinophilic folliculitis; HIV-associated, classic type (also called Ofuji syndrome) and the infancy-associated type.

question: A 76-vear old man presented with a 6-month history of a slowly growing plaque on the forehead. Examination showed a purplish plaque mimicking a bruise with some vascular-looking pa pules. A biopsy showed a tumour arising from the vascular bed with marked atypia and mitoses. The most likely diagnosis is
explanation: Angiosarcoma is an aggressive vascular tumour with high recurrence rate and potential for metastasis to the lung, liver and brain. The 3 clinical settings of angiosarcoma are: (i) in the elderly (predominantly head and neck}, (ii} at sites of lymphoedema, and (iii} radiotherapy-related. Kaposi s sarcoma is in the differential but there is no atypia and the tumour arises from both the endothelial and spindle cells and unlike angiosarcoma, shows positivity for HHV 8. 289 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: A 5-year old girl attends clinic with her parents. She has short and uneven blonde hair with areas of "hair thinning". Her mother is concerned as she has not had a haircut for over 2 years and her hair seem to fall off easily. There is no family history of any hair abnormalities. Hair pull test was positive with multiple hairs pulled off easily. Microscopic examination of the hair showed absence of inner or outer root sheath and distorted hair bulbs. The diagnosis is
explanation: The differential diagnosis includes short anagen syndrome but the hair pull test would be negative. Pili torti is a malformation of the hair shaft which is twisted about its axis. The hair is brittle and short and may be inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. - Monilethrix is an autosomal dominant hair disorder in which the hair shaft is beaded and fragile.

question: You were asked to see a 3-week old baby born through forceps delivery. The paediatrician is concerned about a firm area on his upper back. Examination showed a mobile, firm, subcutaneous plaque. A biopsy taken by a paediatric dermatologist showed areas of necrosis in the adipocytes. The most important biochemical marker that needs regular monitoring is
explanation: rhe diagnosis is subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn, often occurring following traumatic delivery. Hypercalcaemla can occur and serum calcium levels need to be monitored. Signs of hypercalcaemia in a baby include poor feeding, irritability and vomiting.

question: A 45-year old patient is commenced on methotrexate for his psoriasis. The action mode of methotrexate is by binding to
explanation: Binding of methotrexate to dihdrofolate reductase results in the inhibition of the intracellular reduction of folate to tetrahydrofolate which in turn blocks the production of thymidine and purine biosynthesis. The above process also leads to the inhibition of adhesion molecules and cytokines. Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase is blocked by the drug mycophenolate mofetil which leads to the inhibition of the de nova biosynthesis of purines, leading to a reduction In DNA synthesis, nitric oxide production and adhesion molecules. 290 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: A 15-year old boy from Tunisia presented with a palmo-plantar keratoderma and recurrent episodes of impetigo. He had suffered severe periodontitis at the age of 3 and as a consequence has lost most of his teeth. His nails were unaffected. His sister and mother had similar presentations. Both his parents are first cousins. The most likely diagnosis is
explanation: Papillon-Lefevre syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder that presents with palmo-plantar keraoderma, periodontitis and recurrent skin infections. In some cases hearing loss may occur. In pachonychia congenital (PC) the nails are always abnormal (thickened and curved) in addition to the presence of palmo-plantar keratoderma. Two types of this autosomal dominant condition exist: PC-1 and PC-2. In PC-1 (also called Jadassohn-Lewandowsky type ), leukoplakia and follicular keratosis occur in addition to the PPK and nail abnormality. In PC-2 (also called Jackson-Lawler type ), the affected patients have natal teeth and cutaneous cysts (no leukoplakia and/or follicular keratosis). Huriez syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant disorder in which palmo-plantar keratoderma is associated with sclerodactly and a high incidence of squamous cell carcinomas.

question: A 30-year old man is diagnosed with Fabry's disease by the metabolic medicine consultant. Which of the following type of angiokeratomas is associated with Fabry's disease?
explanation: These are the 5 types of angiokeratomas. Angiokeratomas corporis diffusum is associated with Fabry s disease and often presents with multiple tiny angiokeratomas on the trunk and thighs. Angiokeratomas of Mibelli occur on the dorsal aspects of the fingers and toes; whereas angiokeratomas of Fordyce occurs on the vulva or scrotum. Angiokeratoma circumscriptum presents at birth or early in life (predominantly on the legs) as a large unilateral hyperkeratotic plaque with confluent keratotic papules.

question: You refer a patient on long-term hydroxychloroquine to an ophthalmologist as he complains of some visual disturbances. Long-term, high doses of hydroxychloroqulne can give rise to which ocular pathology?
explanation: The anti-malarial drug hydroxychloroquine is useful in cutaneous lupus. Ocular toxicity can occur, particularly if doses exceed 6.5 mg/kg daily. Regular ophthalmic examination which includes Amsler chart reading is mandatory. Mepacrine, a drug often used in conjunction with or as a substitute of hydroxychloroquine does not cause ocular toxicity. 291 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: A 23-year old woman complains of an eczematous eruption on her face, which has been present for over a year and tends to worsen in the summer. She has noticed that the application of some sunscreens worsen her facial eczema. The most appropriate investigation would be
explanation: The history and symptoms are suggestive of a photo-contact allergy in which the combination of a chemical (e.g. sunscreen) and ultraviolet light leads to an allergic contact dermatitis. Although patch testing would be indicated to exclude any contact allergy to the perfume, preservative or any chemical in the sunscreen, photo-patch testing is the investigation needed in suspected photo-contact allergy. Skin prick and RAST testing are useful in detecting type-1 allergy and are therefore not applicable in this setting.

question: In which of the following is the risk of developing squamous cell carcinomas the highest?
explanation: Multiple factors contribute to the development of squamous cell carcinomas, such as immunosuppression, ultraviolet therapy, chronic wounds, arsenic Ingestion, pre- existent dysplastic lesions and previous radiotherapy. The risk of developing skin cancers following treatment with PUVA Is higher than that compared to UVB and this risk is particularly high when PUVA Is administered in a patient who was previously treated with ciclosporin.

question: A 4-year old girl suffers from joint hypermobility, easy bruising and the tendency to develop atrophic scarring. Her father suffered from the same condition and died at the age of 46. Genetic testing showed a mutation on the gene COLPQAl. Which of the following investigations Is highly recommended in this child?
explanation: The history and findings here are suggestive of Ehlers-Danlos (EDS) type IV which is an autosomal dominant condition. This is a vascular type of EDS with the risk of aortic dissection/rupture. Echocardiography is essential in those patients.

question: You plan to commence your patient on ciclosporin. The mode of action of ciclosporin is through binding to
explanation: The binding-complex of ciclosporin and cyclophilin-A inhibits calcineurin which in turn inhibits the migration of transcription factor NFAT (nuclear factor of activated T cells) into the cell nucleus resulting in the inhibition of IL-2. Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase is inhibited by mycophenolate mofetil. Methotrexate binds to dihydrofolate reductase leading to the inhibition of thymidine and purine biosynthesis. CD20 is targeted by the relatively new monoclonal antibody drug rituximab which has been used in lupus and pemphigus. Dihydropteroate synthetase is blocked by dapsone which prevents the formation of folic acid. 292 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: A 23-year old nurse was referred for patch testing as she has noticed the development of an eczematous eruption following the use of plasters or handling any adhesives. The most likely allergen in this case is
explanation: Colophony is found in adhesives and plasters. Primin is the chemical in the plant Primula obconica. Propylene glycol is a preservative found in many products. Benzocaine is found in topical anaesthetics and may cross-react with PPD, PABA and sulphonamides.

question: Which of the following photodermatoses is not seen in children?
explanation: Chronic actinic dermatitis is mostly seen in elderly men, although women and young adults may also be affected. It Is not seen in children and the condition is often persistent. Multiple contact allergies are often associated with the condition.

question: Which of the following photosensitive disorders is least likely to give symptoms shortly following exposure to UV or visible light?
explanation: Lupus erythematosus, actinic prurigo and hydroa vacciniforme do not generally give immediate symptoms following exposure to light. Polymorphic light eruption (PLE) typically has a latency period of several hours but a less common variant exist in which short exposure to light triggers the rash (rapid onset PLE). Drugs should always be included in the differential of immediate photosensitivity, particularly if the symptoms occur in a patient who previously could tolerate UV and visible light exposure.

question: Which of the following genodermatoses is not inherited in an X-linked dominant fashion?
explanation: Dyskeratosis congentia is an X-linked recessive disorder. Incontinentia pigmenti, Goltz syndrome, Conradl-Hunermann syndrome, Bazex syndrome, CHILD and MIDAS are some of the other X-llnked dominant dermatological syndromes. 293 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: You are asked to see a premature neonate as he is born encased in shiny yellow covering. What is the most likely underlying dermatological condition?
explanation: Collodion babies are usually premature and are born encased in skin resembling a yellow, tight and shiny film. Desquamation is usually complete by 2 to 3 weeks by which time the underlying skin disorder reveals itself. The most common underlying diseases are lamellar ichthyosis and non-bullous congenital erythroderma. Rarer conditions include Sjogren-Larsen syndrome, Dorfman-Chanarin syndrome (Neutral lipid storage disease), Gaucher s disease type-2, Trichothyodystrophy, Netherton syndrome, Hay-Well syndrome and Ectodermal dysplasias.

question: A 7-month old boy presents with an itchy red rash on the skin that has been diagnosed as atopic dermatitis. He also has a distinctive circular scaling on the trunk. He was born with widespread red scaly skin. Examination of the scalp hair shows it to be short, spiky, lustreless and brittle. What is the hair abnormality in this condition?
explanation: The clinical features described above are those of Netherton syndrome. Patients are erythrodermic at birth and later develop ichthyosis- ichthyosis linearis circumflexa -circular scaling on the skin and a changing margin. Trlchorrhexls invaginata or Bamboo hair -refers to ball-and-socket-type hair-shaft deformity, which results in sparse, short, spiky, lustreless and brittle hair. Allergic manifestations are commonly present. These include food allergies, hay fever, asthma, atopic eczema, angioedema and urticaria.

question: A 55-year-old diabetic presents with an asymptomatic erythematous rash on both axillae. Wood's light examination shows coral red fluorescence. Which chemical is responsible for this fluorescence?
explanation: Erythrasma is caused by the Gram positive bacterium Corynebacterium minutissimum. The patches of erythrasma display coral red fluoresence on Wood s lamp examination. This is secondary to coproporphyrin Ill production by Corynebacterium minutissimum. 294 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: A 12-month old girl presents with subungual hyperkeratosis lifting the right little finger nail from the nail bed. She was born with a vesicular rash on her right forearm and hand. Which of the following stages in the condition is most likely to follow next?
explanation: Incontinentia pigmenti is an X-linked dominant neurocutaneous syndrome. Cutaneous features are seen in the following stages: - Stage 1 (vesicular) - present at birth or develop within the first 2 weeks of life in the vast majority. Red papules and vesicles on an erythematous base along Blaschko s lines and seen prP.dominantly on the extremities. - Stage 2 (verrucous) - develop in the first few weeks to months of life and resolve over weeks to months. Thickened, warty-appearing linear and whorled plaques on an erythematous base along Blaschko s lines. - Stage 3 (hyperpigmented)- streaks and whorls of brown or slate- gray pigmentation along Blaschko s lines. The location of the hyperpigmented lesions do not correlate with areas of prior skin involvement. - Stage 4 (atrophic/hypopigmented) - develop during adolescence and persist into adulthood. Hypopigmented, atrophic, and reticulate or linear patches can be observed on the lower extremities. Besides cutaneous lesions, patients may have neurologic, ophthalmologic, and dental manifestations. Mutations in the NEMO/IKK-gamma gene, on chromosome Xq28 are responsible for incontinentia pigmenti.

question: A 13-year old girl presents with multiple skin-colored nodules. In addition she has numerous coffee-coloured patches and macules on her skin. Her mother has similar coffee-coloured patches and macules. You diagnose the condition as neurofibromatosis type-1 (NF-1}. Her mother is concerned about the risk of malignancy. Which of the following is the commonest malignancy in NF-1?
explanation: The most common malignancy in NF-1 is neurofibrosarcoma. Other malignancies include phaeochromocytoma, leukaemia, Wilm s tumour and rhabdomyosarcoma.

question: A 20-year old man presents with facial angiofibromas and flesh-coloured plaques on the back. He is under the care of the neurologists for epilepsy. What is the earliest skin sign of this condition?
explanation: Tuberous sclerosis is a neurocutaneous disorder with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. The earliest skin sign in tuberous sclerosis Is hypomelanotic macules. Facial angiofibromas appear at the age of 4-9 years. Peri-ungual and subungual fibromas develop at or after puberty. ,.., Shagreen patch refers to an irregularly thickened, slightly elevated, flesh-coloured plaque, most commonly over the lumbosacral area. It develops in late childhood or adolescence. 295 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: A 20-year old man presents with facial anglofibromas, hypomelanotic macules and flesh-coloured plaques on the back. He is under the care of the neurologists for epilepsy. The hypomelanotic macules appear polygonal or ash leaf in shape under Wood's light examination. What is the histological defect accounting for the hypomelanotic macules in this condition?
explanation: Abnormal melanin synthesis and impaired melanosome transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes accounts for the hypomelanotic macules seen in tuberous sclerosis. These macules are best seen with Wood s light examination and appear polygonal or ash leaf shaped.

question: Which of the following is the gold standard in the diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita?
explanation: Although all the listed options are helpful in establishing the diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita by differentiating it from other immunobullous disorders like bullous pemphigoid, immuno-electron microscopy still remains the gold standard in the diagnosis of epidermolysis bullosa acquisita. Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita lesions have immune deposits within the sub-lamina densa zone of basement membrane zone. Deposits in bullous pemphigoid are higher up in the hemidesmosome area or the lamina lucida area of the basement membrane. In cicatricial pemphigoid, antigenic targets are confined to the lamina lucida. Western blots of human skin basement membrane proteins contain type VII collagen. A new ELISA developed from recombinant, purified, post-translationally modified NC-1 in stably transfected human cells is considered more sensitive than immunofluorescence and Western blotting and very specific for antibodies to type VII collagen.

question: Which one of the following forms of pemphigus involves non-stratified squamous epithelium?
explanation: Paraneoplastic pemphigus is the only form of pemphigus that has involvement of non-stratified squamous epithelium.

question: Which of the following is not seen at an increased incidence in dermatitis herpetiformis?
explanation: Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with an increased risk for the following: - Gastrointestinal diseases, including: achlorhydria, atrophic gastritis, pernicious anaemia, coeliac disease, malabsorption and bone loss. - Malignancies, including: gastrointestinal and non-Hodgkin s lymphomas. -Auto-immune diseases, including: thyroid disease, insulin- dependent diabetes, lupus erythematosus, Sjogren s syndrome, and vitiligo. - Neurologic diseases, including: epilepsy, ataxia, and dementia. 296 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: One of the following is not an inherited form of epidermolysis bullosa?
explanation: Inherited epid rmolysis bullosa (EB) is subclassified according to the level of skin separation seen in skin blisters on transmission electron microscopic analysis. - EB Simplex - intra-epidermal blistering associated with keratin gene mutations. - Hemidesmosomal EB - blistering skin disease with a level of separation that is intermediate between EB simplex and junctional EB. - Junctional EB - blister formation within the lamina lucida of the basement membrane zone due to defects of anchoring filaments. - Dystrophic EB - defects of the anchoring fibril, which results in s ublamina densa separation.

question: Which of the following is characterized by the development of peri-orificial granulation tissue?
explanation: Lethal junctional epidermolysis bullosa or Herlitz junctional epidermolysis bullosa patients is a life threatening disease. Death rates of up to 40 % are seen in the first year of life and most of the surviving patients succumb before the age of 5 years. Lethal junctional epidermolysis bullosa is characterized by generalized extensive blistering at birth. Patients develop peri-orificial granulation tissue in infancy.

question: Which of the following is the least common subtype of morphoea?
explanation: Plaque-type morphea is the commonest subtype of morphoea. Other subtypes in decreasing order of frequency include: - Linear scleroderma; - Generalized morphea; - Parry-Romberg syndrome; - En coup de Sabre. Morphea profunda, guttate morphoea, bullous morphea, keloidal morphoea and pansclerotic morphea of childhood are other rare forms of morphoea. 297 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: Auto-antibodies can be seen in morphea. Which of the following is not associated with auto-antibody positivity in morphoea?
explanation: Serum auto-antibodies have been found with variable frequency in patients with localized scleroderma. Anti-nuclear antibodies usually with a homogenous immunofluorescence pattern are most commonly found. Anti-single stranded DNA and/or anti-histone antibodies may be found with extensive involvement. Compared with other subsets of localized scleroderma, patients with generalized morphea have a higher frequency of antibody positivity which correlates with a more severe clinical presentation, greater number of lesions, more sclerotic lesions and longer duration of clinical course.

question: Which of the following is not a recognized risk factor for development of Dupuytren's contracture?
explanation: Dupuytren s contracture (palmar fibromatosis) is a fibroproliferative disease . ..., Bilateral, progressive fibrosis of the pal mar fascia. Presenting most commonly as nodules over the fourth and fifth metacarpal head. Joint contractures and flexion deformities may follow. Significant risk factors for development of Dupuytren s contracture include old age, male sex (three to four fold increase), white northern European ancestry, family history, seizures, alcohol-induced liver disease, trauma, smoking, and diabetes mellitus.

question: Which of the following syndromes has desmoid syndrome as an associated feature?
explanation: Desmoid tumours are deep-seated, aggressive, low-grade clonal benign musculoaponeurotic fibromatoses. They have an infiltrative growth pattern and locally recur, but do not metastasize. They have a mutation in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene (5q21) and are associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) syndrome and Gardner s syndrome. They are classified as extra-abdominal or intra-abdominal. Intra-abdominal desmoids have been associated in 10 to 15 % of patients with FAP and Gardner s syndrome, with the latter usually presenting as retroperitoneal tumors. 298 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: Which of the following is not a recognized risk factor for Peyronie's disease?
explanation: Peyronie s disease is fibrosis of the fibrous septa between the corpus spongiosum and the corpora cavernosa along the dorsum of the penis. It is often associated with Dupuytren s contracture. Risk factors include genetic predisposition, trauma to the penis, systemic vascular diseases, smoking and alcohol consumption.

question: All of these can be presenting features of Bazex syndrome except which one?
explanation: Bazex syndrome is an X-linked dominant syndrome, which is characterized by follicular atrophoderma, multiple basal cell carcinomas, hypotrichosis, and localized hypohidrosis. The follicular atrophoderma presents as multiple ice-pick marks or patulous follicles (most commonly on the dorsal sides of the hands). Associated findings may include facial hyperpigmentation, milia, hair shaft dystrophy, and multiple genital trichoepitheliomas.

question: Which of the following is associated with elastosis perforans serpiginosa?
explanation: Elastosis perforans serpiginosa is a perforating disorder characterized by transepidermal elimination of elastic fibers. Hyperkeratotic papules varying from 2 mm to 1 cm in diameter occur in a serpiginous distribution. D-penicillamine is associated with the development of elastosis perforans serpiginosa. The neck is most commonly involved.

question: Which of the following disorders gives an erythema contusiforme appearance?
explanation: The tender erythematous warm nodules and raised plaques of erythema nodosum evolve into red or purplish colour to a yellow or greenish discoloration, resembling a deep bruise- erythema contusiforme. 299 Section 3: Answers & Comments

question: Which of the following panniculitides can demonstrate an isomorphic phenomenon?
explanation: Lupus panniculitis is a chronic recurrent panniculitis. It is a mild variant of lupus erythematosus. It is more frequent in women than men. May present as subcutaneous nodules as the only clinical manifestation of the disease. Histological features of discoid lupus erythematosus at the dermal-epidermal junction may be seen in only 20-30% patients. Lobular panniculitis without vasculitis is the predominant histopathological feature. An isomorphic phenomenon (Koebner) is frequently seen in patients with lupus panniculitis. Subcutaneous erythematous nodules often develop or recur at the sites of trauma. Treatments include topical, intralesional or oral corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine and dapsone. An isomorphic phenomenon is also frequent In al-antitr ypsin- deficiency-associated panniculitis.

question: Elevated levels of which of the following enzymes is predominantly implicated in pancreatic panniculitis?
explanation: Pancreatic panniculitis is also termed enzymatic fat necrosis. It is associated with several pancreatic diseases, including acute and chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic carcinoma, pancreatic pseudocysts, vasculo-pancreatic fistulae, and drug induced pancreatitis. In some patients there may be no demonstrable pancreatic disease. Pancreatic enzymes, mostly lipase, seem to be responsible for the subcutaneous fat necrosis. Presents as erythematous subcutaneous nodules around the ankles and knees that often ulcerate spontaneously. Histopathologically, mostly lobular panniculitis without vasculitis is evident with an intense necrosis of the adipocytes at the centre of the fat lobules. Ghost adipocytes are necrotic adipocytes, which have lost their nuclei and contain finely granular and basophilic material within their cytoplasm. Ghost cells result from saponification- hydrolytic action of pancreatic enzymes on fat, followed by calcium deposition. These ghost adipocytes are characteristic of pancreatic panniculitis. 300 Settlon 3: Answers & Comments

question: Which of the following phenotypes Is most commonly associated with al- antitrypsin-deficiency panniculitis?
explanation: The four major categories of al-antitrypsin genes include: F (fast), M (medium), S (slow), and Z (very slow). Two alleles determine the specific al-antitrypsin phenotype. The most common allele associated with normal levels of al-antitrypsin is M. Sand Z alleles are associated with low serum levels of the enzyme. zz phenotype has severe al-antitrypsin deficiency. Serious clinical manifestations include emphysema, hepatitis, cirrhosis, vasculitis, and angioedema. Clinical manifestations of panniculitis include subcutaneous nodules on the lower abdomen, buttocks, and proximal extremities. Other features include frequent ulceration and isomorphic phenomenon. Histopathological features include lobular panniculitis without vasculitis, necrosis of the fat lobules with a dense inflammatory infiltrate of neutrophils. Dapsone is the mainstay treatment for mild disease. For severe forms of the disease: intravenous infusion of exogenous al-proteinase inhibitor concentrate or genetically engineered crl-antitrypsin can be used.

question: Which of the following is the commonest auto-immune disorder associated with vitiligo?
explanation: Vitiligo is frequently associated with auto-immune disorders. The commonest is thyroid dysfunction, either hyperthyroidism (Graves disease) or hypothyroidism (Hashimoto s thyroiditis). Other auto-immune disorders associated with vitiligo include Addison s disease, pernicious anemia, alopecia areata, and diabetes mellitus. Patients with auto-immune polyendocrinopathy candidiasis ectodermal dystrophy also have an increased prevalence of vitiligo. 301 Section 1: Practice Questions i References .. . . - 1.
